title: OpenRiak KV 3.4.0
text: OpenRiak KV is a distributed key-value database for applications that need to store and retrieve data across several servers. Its replica policies and conflict handling let applications make explicit choices about availability and consistency.

title: OpenRiak KV 3.4.0
heading: Start learning#
text: New to OpenRiak? Read What OpenRiak KV is, then follow Build and explore a Docker cluster to build a disposable cluster and make your first request.

title: OpenRiak KV 3.4.0
heading: Choose your next task#
text: Foundations: understand the data model, architecture, and operational trade-offs. Tutorials: work through guided exercises with observable results. How-to: complete a specific installation, application, maintenance, or recovery task. Reference: find settings, commands, API fields, and compatibility limits.

text: Choose the package that matches your operating system and architecture on the downloads page. Existing deployments should follow Upgrade an OpenRiak KV cluster before changing a cluster member’s package.

title: Membership, gossip, and handoff
text: Cluster membership records which nodes participate and how partitions are owned. Gossip spreads ring information between nodes; handoff moves the data needed when ownership changes.

title: Membership, gossip, and handoff
heading: Agreement and movement are separate#
text: A planned join, leave, or replacement changes the intended ownership. Reviewing and committing the plan establishes the transition to perform. Data still has to move, so membership state and handoff progress must both be checked before treating the operation as complete.

title: Membership, gossip, and handoff
heading: Handoff during normal changes and failures#
text: Ownership handoff transfers a partition to its new permanent owner. Hinted handoff returns work held by a fallback node after a primary node recovers. Repair transfers can reconstruct data from surviving replicas.

title: Membership, gossip, and handoff
heading: Handoff during normal changes and failures#
text: Hinted handoff returns work held by a fallback node after a primary node recovers. Repair transfers can reconstruct data from surviving replicas. These activities share resources with application requests, even though their purposes differ.

title: Membership, gossip, and handoff
heading: Why one change affects other work#
text: Moving partitions consumes disk and network capacity and changes the set of processes serving the affected data. Overlapping maintenance can remove copies that are still needed for a previous recovery. Pausing or limiting transfers can protect client latency, but it also extends the period before placement settles.

title: Replica placement and failure domains
text: Replica placement determines which failures can remove all copies of an object. Copies on different partitions are useful only to the extent that their physical nodes and failure domains remain independent.

title: Replica placement and failure domains
heading: Partitions, nodes, and locations#
text: An object’s preference list identifies its replica partitions. Placement algorithms distribute ownership across nodes and can take location information into account. A location represents an operational failure boundary, such as a rack or availability zone; it must reflect the deployment’s actual topology.

title: Replica placement and failure domains
heading: Partitions, nodes, and locations#
text: Placement algorithms distribute ownership across nodes and can take location information into account. A location represents an operational failure boundary, such as a rack or availability zone; it must reflect the deployment’s actual topology. When a primary owner is unavailable, a fallback can temporarily accept work under the applicable policy.

title: Replica placement and failure domains
heading: Partitions, nodes, and locations#
text: A location represents an operational failure boundary, such as a rack or availability zone; it must reflect the deployment’s actual topology. When a primary owner is unavailable, a fallback can temporarily accept work under the applicable policy. A fallback copy helps availability, but it is not the same as an acknowledgement from a primary replica.

title: Replica placement and failure domains
heading: Correlated failures#
text: Three example replicas on three machines do not protect against losing the single rack that powers all three. Similarly, replicas in one cluster do not replace off-cluster backups or a tested disaster-recovery strategy.

title: Replica placement and failure domains
heading: Recovery and resource management#
text: After a failure, the surviving nodes must continue serving clients while accepting redistributed work and rebuilding copies. Storage capacity, network bandwidth, and backend write capacity must include that recovery load. Running every node at its steady-state limit leaves no margin for repair.

title: Replica placement and failure domains
heading: Recovery and resource management#
text: Storage capacity, network bandwidth, and backend write capacity must include that recovery load. Running every node at its steady-state limit leaves no margin for repair. It is generally recommended that nodes consume no more than 70% of their total resources for day-to-day use, allowing the remaining 30% for failure state recovery.

title: Rings, partitions, and virtual nodes
text: The ring divides the keyspace into partitions. A virtual node, or vnode, manages one partition on a physical node. Each physical node normally hosts many vnodes.

title: Rings, partitions, and virtual nodes
heading: From a key to responsible partitions#
text: OpenRiak hashes an object’s bucket and key to locate it on the ring. A preference list identifies the partitions responsible for replicas. Different objects spread across those partitions, distributing storage and request work across the cluster.

title: Rings, partitions, and virtual nodes
heading: From a key to responsible partitions#
text: A preference list identifies the partitions responsible for replicas. Different objects spread across those partitions, distributing storage and request work across the cluster. A vnode is an Erlang process with a backend store and partition-specific responsibilities.

title: Rings, partitions, and virtual nodes
heading: From a key to responsible partitions#
text: Different objects spread across those partitions, distributing storage and request work across the cluster. A vnode is an Erlang process with a backend store and partition-specific responsibilities. Adding a physical node redistributes partition ownership; it does not create a new ring for each node.

title: Rings, partitions, and virtual nodes
heading: Ring size and node count#
text: Ring size fixes the number of partitions in the cluster. Node count determines how those partitions are shared across the nodes. More partitions can allow finer placement, but also add stores, processes, trees, and maintenance work.

title: Rings, partitions, and virtual nodes
heading: Ring size and node count#
text: Node count determines how those partitions are shared across the nodes. More partitions can allow finer placement, but also add stores, processes, trees, and maintenance work. Ring size is therefore an initial deployment decision, not a request-level performance switch.

title: Rings, partitions, and virtual nodes
heading: Ownership changes#
text: During a membership change, the old owner transfers partition data to the new owner through handoff. A node appearing in membership does not mean all data transfers have completed. Temporary fallback ownership during a failure is also distinct from permanent membership.

title: Rings, partitions, and virtual nodes
heading: Ownership changes#
text: A node appearing in membership does not mean all data transfers have completed. Temporary fallback ownership during a failure is also distinct from permanent membership. The ring is a placement structure; it does not impose a global order on object updates.

title: The lifecycle of a read and a write
text: A client can send an object request to a reachable OpenRiak node. That node coordinates work with the vnodes responsible for the object’s replicas; it need not own the object’s primary partition.

title: The lifecycle of a read and a write
heading: A write#
text: The coordinator interprets the namespace, bucket policy, causal context, and request options. It sends work to the relevant replicas and waits for the acknowledgements requested by the client. When those conditions are met, it can return success while other work is still in progress.

title: The lifecycle of a read and a write
heading: A write#
text: It sends work to the relevant replicas and waits for the acknowledgements requested by the client. When those conditions are met, it can return success while other work is still in progress. A timeout means the client did not receive the required success within the time limit.

title: The lifecycle of a read and a write
heading: A write#
text: When those conditions are met, it can return success while other work is still in progress. A timeout means the client did not receive the required success within the time limit. It does not prove that no replica accepted the write.

title: The lifecycle of a read and a write
heading: A write#
text: A timeout means the client did not receive the required success within the time limit. It does not prove that no replica accepted the write. Retrying without preserving the application’s identity and update context can create duplicate work or conflicting values.

title: The lifecycle of a read and a write
heading: A read#
text: The coordinator requests replica responses, reconciles the versions it receives, and returns a value, siblings, a missing-object response, or an error. The result depends on the policy and the responses available for that request. Read repair can update replicas found to be stale.

title: The lifecycle of a read and a write
heading: Example: A slow replica#
text: If enough replicas acknowledge a write while another is slow, the client may receive success before every copy is updated. A later request can encounter the difference. Read repair and anti-entropy will help replicas converge; while application conflict handling deals with changes that are concurrent rather than merely late.

title: Backups, restores, and disaster recovery
text: A backup preserves a recoverable state independently of the current cluster. Replication maintains another evolving copy; it can also carry accidental updates and deletions.

title: Backups, restores, and disaster recovery
heading: Match the backup to the backend#
text: Backend files, ring state, configuration, and cluster metadata have different consistency requirements. Copying a changing directory is not the same as a usable backup. The supported procedure depends on whether the node or backend can provide a consistent view for the copy.

title: Backups, restores, and disaster recovery
heading: Define the recovery target#
text: Restoring one node into a surviving cluster differs from reconstructing a whole cluster. In the first case, later surviving versions may need to repair the restored copy. In the second, the available backups determine which data and history can be recovered.

title: Backups, restores, and disaster recovery
heading: Define the recovery target#
text: In the first case, later surviving versions may need to repair the restored copy. In the second, the available backups determine which data and history can be recovered. Older backups can contain values whose deletion markers have since been reaped.

title: Backups, restores, and disaster recovery
heading: Define the recovery target#
text: In the second, the available backups determine which data and history can be recovered. Older backups can contain values whose deletion markers have since been reaped. Reintroducing them without a reconciliation plan can resurrect deleted data.

title: Backups, restores, and disaster recovery
heading: Test the restore#
text: A completed backup job is evidence that a copy was made, not that applications can recover from it. Test restoration in an isolated environment and check object content, metadata, indexes, security configuration, and required cluster identity information. Record the recovery duration and the data interval that would be lost.

title: Failure and recovery
text: A node failure changes which replicas are reachable and which work the surviving nodes in the cluster must perform. Recovery is complete only when service, data, and replica placement have been checked.

title: Failure and recovery
heading: Temporary loss#
text: During a short interruption, eligible requests may use a mix of available primary and fallback nodes. Whether they succeed depends on their acknowledgement requirements. Restoring connectivity does not immediately establish that all copies agree; hinted handoff, read repair, and anti-entropy still have work to do.

title: Failure and recovery
heading: Permanent loss#
text: A failed node may require replacement and reconstruction from surviving replicas. The decision depends on the state of its disks and identity, the remaining copies, and the current membership plan. Reusing a name or clearing a data directory without understanding that state can complicate recovery and even lead to further loss of data.

title: Failure and recovery
heading: Widespread failure#
text: If surviving copies cannot supply the dataset, recovery needs a suitable backup or another independently recoverable source. Replication does not recover information that has been lost everywhere.

title: Failure and recovery
heading: What to verify#
text: Check membership agreement, ownership transfers, backend health, representative reads and writes, and repair progress. An available HTTP listener proves only one part of recovery. Retain evidence of the original failure until the cause and the recovered state are understood.

title: Mixed versions, capabilities, and upgrade boundaries
text: A rolling upgrade creates a period in which some nodes in a cluster run different software. Compatibility must cover their communication, stored data, negotiated capabilities, and Erlang/OTP runtimes.

title: Mixed versions, capabilities, and upgrade boundaries
heading: Capability negotiation#
text: Nodes can negotiate features that require cluster-wide agreement. A feature available on the new binary may remain inactive until the participating nodes support it. Negotiation is a compatibility mechanism, not proof that every historical version can join every newer cluster.

title: Mixed versions, capabilities, and upgrade boundaries
heading: Persistent changes matter#
text: A newer release can write data or metadata that older software cannot interpret. Enabling a feature may therefore change the available rollback path. Reinstalling an old package alone is not a general downgrade procedure.

title: Mixed versions, capabilities, and upgrade boundaries
heading: Runtime and backend boundaries#
text: Erlang distribution compatibility and backend file formats constrain the route between releases. Review the exact source and target versions, package runtime, compression choices, and activated features. Do not skip intermediate steps merely because the application protocol appears unchanged.

title: Mixed versions, capabilities, and upgrade boundaries
heading: Configuration during an upgrade#
text: A preserved configuration file can retain explicit old values when package defaults change. Compare the installed configuration with the release’s generated settings, and record deliberate overrides separately. Validate the upgrade and recovery path against representative data before advancing through the production cluster.

title: Rolling maintenance and recovery headroom
text: Rolling maintenance keeps part of a cluster serving traffic while nodes are changed in stages. Its success depends on spare capacity and on waiting for recovery between stages.

title: Rolling maintenance and recovery headroom
heading: A rolling change is a sequence#
text: Stopping a node reduces the available placement and shifts requests to survivors. Restarting it restores a process but is not the end of the sequence, but handoff and repair may still be catching up. Starting the next stage too early can overlap those reduced-redundancy periods.

title: Rolling maintenance and recovery headroom
heading: Define a completion state#
text: A useful gate includes application health, membership state, relevant handoffs, replication and repair progress, and resource pressure. A service manager reporting “running” is insufficient on its own.

title: Rolling maintenance and recovery headroom
heading: Failure domains affect the sequence#
text: Placement across locations can support maintenance strategies that account for a whole domain. That requires verified placement and enough surviving capacity; it is not permission to stop an arbitrary group of nodes together.

title: Rolling maintenance and recovery headroom
heading: Preserve a buffer for an unexpected failure#
text: Maintenance is not the only event the cluster may experience. A second failure, slow disk, or replication backlog can occur during a planned change. Size and schedule the operation so that the agreed application requirements still hold, and stop advancing if completion fails.

title: Rolling maintenance and recovery headroom
heading: Preserve a buffer for an unexpected failure#
text: A second failure, slow disk, or replication backlog can occur during a planned change. Size and schedule the operation so that the agreed application requirements still hold, and stop advancing if completion fails. It is generally recommended to maintain a 30% buffer in resource consumption to allow for failures.

title: Bucket types and data policies
text: Bucket types group buckets under a named namespace and shared properties. They let an application make data-policy choices explicitly instead of relying on one cluster-wide policy for every object.

title: Bucket types and data policies
heading: Policies belong to the data model#
text: Replica count, acknowledgement behaviour, sibling handling, and data-type selection affect the contract an application implements. A bucket for mergeable counters has different requirements from a bucket for arbitrary binary objects. Select the policy before writing application data.

title: Bucket types and data policies
heading: Creation and activation#
text: A type is created, validated, and activated before clients use its namespace. Activation makes the type usable; it is not a migration of objects from an untyped bucket. Applications must include the type in subsequent requests.

title: Bucket types and data policies
heading: Creation and activation#
text: Activation makes the type usable; it is not a migration of objects from an untyped bucket. Applications must include the type in subsequent requests. Not every property can be changed safely after activation.

title: Bucket types and data policies
heading: Creation and activation#
text: Applications must include the type in subsequent requests. Not every property can be changed safely after activation. Some combinations are constrained by the data type or backend.

title: Bucket types and data policies
heading: Creation and activation#
text: Not every property can be changed safely after activation. Some combinations are constrained by the data type or backend. The bucket-property reference records the applicable fields and constraints.

title: Bucket types and data policies
heading: Policy changes do not rewrite history#
text: Changing how future writes are handled does not resolve existing siblings, convert stored objects into another data type, or move data to a different backend. Such changes require an explicit data migration and verification plan. You should ensure that policy definitions remain under configuration management, and verify client behaviour against the resolved effective properties of the designated namespace.

title: Causality, version vectors, and siblings
text: Causal context records which object history a write has observed. OpenRiak uses version information to distinguish a later update from an update made independently of another writer.

title: Causality, version vectors, and siblings
heading: Read, modify, and preserve context#
text: A client reads an object and receives its context. Returning that context with the next write lets the database relate the new value to the versions the client saw. Treat the encoded context as opaque; copying a timestamp or an ETag into its place is not equivalent.

title: Causality, version vectors, and siblings
heading: Concurrent writes#
text: Suppose two clients read the same profile and each makes a different edit. Neither write has observed the other. With sibling-preserving policy, both contents can survive as siblings.

title: Causality, version vectors, and siblings
heading: Concurrent writes#
text: Neither write has observed the other. With sibling-preserving policy, both contents can survive as siblings. They share one object identity; they are not two independently keyed records.

title: Causality, version vectors, and siblings
heading: Concurrent writes#
text: With sibling-preserving policy, both contents can survive as siblings. They share one object identity; they are not two independently keyed records. Resolving siblings means applying an merge rule at the application level and writing the combined value with the context covering the versions being resolved.

title: Causality, version vectors, and siblings
heading: Concurrent writes#
text: They share one object identity; they are not two independently keyed records. Resolving siblings means applying an merge rule at the application level and writing the combined value with the context covering the versions being resolved. A fresh concurrent update can still arrive while that happens.

title: Causality, version vectors, and siblings
heading: Missing context#
text: A blind overwrite discards information needed to distinguish an intentional replacement from an independent update. The consequences depend on bucket policy, but the client should not assume it has safely superseded all earlier work. Version metadata is also used by repair to compare replicas.

title: Causality, version vectors, and siblings
heading: Missing context#
text: The consequences depend on bucket policy, but the client should not assume it has safely superseded all earlier work. Version metadata is also used by repair to compare replicas. Matching wall-clock timestamps alone cannot establish the same causal relationship.

title: Conditional updates and latch objects
text: Conditional updates check that an object is absent or still has the state a client observed before accepting a change. They reduce common update races but do not give ordinary OpenRiak objects a formal strong-consistency guarantee.

title: Conditional updates and latch objects
heading: Checks and coordination#
text: An API-only check can race with a concurrent write. Token-based modes coordinate conditional writers more closely, with different placement and failure assumptions. Token waits can expire, unconditioned writers do not participate, and separate clusters do not share a token grant.

title: Conditional updates and latch objects
heading: Checks and coordination#
text: Token-based modes coordinate conditional writers more closely, with different placement and failure assumptions. Token waits can expire, unconditioned writers do not participate, and separate clusters do not share a token grant.
