title: Conditional updates and latch objects
heading: Latch objects#
text: A latch is an application-chosen object used to coordinate a larger activity. For example, workers can conditionally create a marker before claiming a batch. The marker does not atomically include the batch’s other writes, and a worker can fail after creating it.

title: Conditional updates and latch objects
heading: Latch objects#
text: For example, workers can conditionally create a marker before claiming a batch. The marker does not atomically include the batch’s other writes, and a worker can fail after creating it. The application therefore needs an ownership, expiry or recovery rule and must handle uncertain outcomes.

title: Conditional updates and latch objects
heading: Latch objects#
text: The marker does not atomically include the batch’s other writes, and a worker can fail after creating it. The application therefore needs an ownership, expiry or recovery rule and must handle uncertain outcomes. A latch should not be treated as a distributed lock with stronger guarantees than the conditional request itself.

title: Conditional updates and latch objects
heading: Conflicts remain possible#
text: You should preserve the causal context, enforce precondition‑failure handling, and maintain a defined conflict‑resolution strategy. Routine concurrent writes, network partitions, operational maintenance, or active/active multi‑cluster traffic can invalidate any assumptions derived from a previously successful condition check.

title: Conflict-free replicated data types
text: Conflict-free replicated data types define operations whose concurrent effects can be merged. They are useful when the application’s required behaviour matches the supplied counter, set, map, grow-only set, or HyperLogLog semantics.

title: Conflict-free replicated data types
heading: Operations carry meaning#
text: Incrementing a distributed counter expresses a change, rather than replacing the last value the client read. Concurrent increments can therefore be combined. Set additions and removals have their own rules; removing an observed member is different from replacing an entire collection with a local snapshot.

title: Conflict-free replicated data types
heading: Operations carry meaning#
text: Concurrent increments can therefore be combined. Set additions and removals have their own rules; removing an observed member is different from replacing an entire collection with a local snapshot. Maps contain typed fields whose changes can be merged using the field’s data-type semantics.

title: Conflict-free replicated data types
heading: Operations carry meaning#
text: Set additions and removals have their own rules; removing an observed member is different from replacing an entire collection with a local snapshot. Maps contain typed fields whose changes can be merged using the field’s data-type semantics. A map is not a transaction spanning unrelated objects.

title: Conflict-free replicated data types
heading: Context still matters#
text: Some operations, particularly removals, need context from a previous fetch. You should preserve that context and use the matching data-type API. An ordinary object PUT is not a substitute for a data-type update.

title: Conflict-free replicated data types
heading: Choose the right structure#
text: A grow-only set cannot remove an element. HyperLogLog estimates distinct observations rather than returning an exact list or exact cardinality. A counter records increments and decrements but does not enforce a non-negative balance across independent writers.

title: Conflict-free replicated data types
heading: Choose the right structure#
text: HyperLogLog estimates distinct observations rather than returning an exact list or exact cardinality. A counter records increments and decrements but does not enforce a non-negative balance across independent writers. These structures remove some application merge work, while retaining the availability and convergence considerations of a replicated system.

title: Deletion, tombstones, and expiration
text: Deleting an object changes its replicated state. The reclamation of disk space used by old values and deletion markers is a separate operation.

title: Deletion, tombstones, and expiration
heading: Tombstones preserve deletion history#
text: A tombstone allows replicas and replication partners to distinguish a deletion from an object they have not yet received. If that history disappears while an older live copy can still return, repair or replication can make the value reappear. Retention must therefore account for offline replicas, replication interruptions, backups, and the time required to reconcile them.

title: Deletion, tombstones, and expiration
heading: Tombstones preserve deletion history#
text: If that history disappears while an older live copy can still return, repair or replication can make the value reappear. Retention must therefore account for offline replicas, replication interruptions, backups, and the time required to reconcile them. A short retention interval cannot compensate for a recovery path that reintroduces older data much later.

title: Deletion, tombstones, and expiration
heading: Expiration and reclamation#
text: Expiration is a policy for making data eligible to expire. Its scope and behaviour depend on the backend and configuration. Reaping removes eligible tombstones; compaction or merging reclaims storage occupied by obsolete records.

title: Deletion, tombstones, and expiration
heading: Expiration and reclamation#
text: Its scope and behaviour depend on the backend and configuration. Reaping removes eligible tombstones; compaction or merging reclaims storage occupied by obsolete records. These mechanisms have different prerequisites and should not be used interchangeably.

title: Deletion, tombstones, and expiration
heading: Application observations#
text: A client can receive a missing-object response while deletion metadata remains stored. Conversely, reducing the number of visible objects does not immediately reduce filesystem usage. Monitoring must distinguish logical data, retained history, and physical storage.

title: Deletion, tombstones, and expiration
heading: Application observations#
text: Conversely, reducing the number of visible objects does not immediately reduce filesystem usage. Monitoring must distinguish logical data, retained history, and physical storage. The creation of a lifecycle policy should be done in tandem with replication and restore procedures, rather than in isolation where the two may conflict.

title: Eventual consistency and convergence
text: Eventual consistency allows replicas to differ temporarily. When updates stop and the required communication and repair work succeeds, replicas can converge on the same object state.

title: Eventual consistency and convergence
heading: Different does not always mean conflicting#
text: A replica may simply be behind: one version causally follows another, and the older copy can be replaced. Two independently created versions may instead be concurrent. Convergence then requires the configured object semantics or the application to combine them.

title: Eventual consistency and convergence
heading: Different does not always mean conflicting#
text: Two independently created versions may instead be concurrent. Convergence then requires the configured object semantics or the application to combine them. Read repair reacts to differences observed during reads.

title: Eventual consistency and convergence
heading: Different does not always mean conflicting#
text: Convergence then requires the configured object semantics or the application to combine them. Read repair reacts to differences observed during reads. Active anti-entropy looks for differences independently of application reads, including objects that are rarely accessed.

title: Eventual consistency and convergence
heading: Different does not always mean conflicting#
text: Read repair reacts to differences observed during reads. Active anti-entropy looks for differences independently of application reads, including objects that are rarely accessed. Replication between clusters adds another asynchronous path with its own queues and reconciliation.

title: Eventual consistency and convergence
heading: What a successful request tells you#
text: A write acknowledgement confirms the request’s acknowledgement conditions, not that all replicas everywhere already contain the result. A read reflects the responses available under its policy. Stronger acknowledgement requirements change the trade-off between availability, latency, and surviving particular failures; they do not automatically provide serial execution.

title: Objects, keys, and buckets
text: An object is a value and its metadata, addressed by a bucket and key. A bucket type can add a namespace and a shared data policy to that address.

title: Objects, keys, and buckets
heading: Keys and values#
text: The key identifies the object within its bucket. Values are byte sequences with metadata such as a media type; a JSON value is an application convention rather than a schema enforced across the bucket. Choose an object boundary that matches what the application reads and updates together.

title: Objects, keys, and buckets
heading: Keys and values#
text: Values are byte sequences with metadata such as a media type; a JSON value is an application convention rather than a schema enforced across the bucket. Choose an object boundary that matches what the application reads and updates together. An object can have multiple concurrent contents, called siblings.

title: Objects, keys, and buckets
heading: Keys and values#
text: Choose an object boundary that matches what the application reads and updates together. An object can have multiple concurrent contents, called siblings. A read is therefore not always a single value, even when the client requested one key.

title: Objects, keys, and buckets
heading: Buckets and types#
text: Buckets group keys and provide a policy scope. A typed bucket is addressed using its type as well as its bucket name. The same textual bucket name under two types identifies two namespaces; dropping the type from a request can make existing data appear missing.

title: Objects, keys, and buckets
heading: A small example#
text: An application might store one customer profile under the example key `customer-42` in a `profiles` bucket. Orders can be separate objects with their own identifiers. That separation avoids rewriting a whole customer history for every order, but the application must coordinate any relationship between those objects.

title: Objects, keys, and buckets
heading: A small example#
text: Orders can be separate objects with their own identifiers. That separation avoids rewriting a whole customer history for every order, but the application must coordinate any relationship between those objects. Indexes support discovering keys by selected attributes.

title: Objects, keys, and buckets
heading: A small example#
text: That separation avoids rewriting a whole customer history for every order, but the application must coordinate any relationship between those objects. Indexes support discovering keys by selected attributes. They do not make a bucket a relational table.

title: Quorums, availability, and durability
text: Request acknowledgements determine how much replica participation a client requires before an operation succeeds. Durability also depends on where those replicas live and what their storage acknowledgements mean.

title: Quorums, availability, and durability
heading: Read and write requirements#
text: Read and write options select the required responses. Primary requirements restrict which responses count; durable-write requirements concern persistence acknowledgements. The effective values come from request options and bucket policy.

title: Quorums, availability, and durability
heading: Read and write requirements#
text: Primary requirements restrict which responses count; durable-write requirements concern persistence acknowledgements. The effective values come from request options and bucket policy. The accepted values are defined in the object-request reference.

title: Quorums, availability, and durability
heading: Read and write requirements#
text: The effective values come from request options and bucket policy. The accepted values are defined in the object-request reference. Consult the generated configuration catalogue for release-specific settings rather than assuming a numerical default.

title: Quorums, availability, and durability
heading: Why overlapping counts are not serial execution#
text: Requiring overlapping read and write response counts can reduce stale observations under suitable assumptions. It does not remove concurrency, fallback placement, partitions, or independent coordination. In particular, quorum arithmetic alone does not turn ordinary OpenRiak operations into strongly consistent transactions.

title: Quorums, availability, and durability
heading: Choosing a trade-off#
text: Higher requirements can make a request fail when fewer replicas are reachable and can expose the latency of slower replicas. Lower requirements can allow progress through more failures but leave more uncertainty about which copies hold the result. For example, an application can choose to reject a critical update when its required primary responses are unavailable.

title: Quorums, availability, and durability
heading: Choosing a trade-off#
text: Lower requirements can allow progress through more failures but leave more uncertainty about which copies hold the result. For example, an application can choose to reject a critical update when its required primary responses are unavailable. That is an explicit application policy, not evidence that the cluster has lost every copy.

title: Resolving concurrent updates
text: Concurrent updates need a rule that reflects the meaning of the application data. OpenRiak can retain siblings so that resolving a conflict does not silently discard an independent change.

title: Resolving concurrent updates
heading: Choose a merge rule before conflicts occur#
text: For a shopping collection, a merge may combine independently added items. For a document, it may require a field-level merge or a user’s decision. Choosing whichever value has the latest timestamp can discard valid work and depends on clocks as well as application semantics.

title: Resolving concurrent updates
heading: Choose a merge rule before conflicts occur#
text: For a document, it may require a field-level merge or a user’s decision. Choosing whichever value has the latest timestamp can discard valid work and depends on clocks as well as application semantics. A good automatic rule is deterministic and remains correct when applied again.

title: Resolving concurrent updates
heading: Choose a merge rule before conflicts occur#
text: Choosing whichever value has the latest timestamp can discard valid work and depends on clocks as well as application semantics. A good automatic rule is deterministic and remains correct when applied again. Where possible, it should give the same result regardless of the order in which replicas or retries present the inputs.

title: Resolving concurrent updates
heading: Resolution is another write#
text: Read all siblings and preserve their combined context. Compute the application’s resolved content and submit a write with that context. If another writer updates the object concurrently, the result can contain another conflict; resolution is not an exclusive lock over future writes.

title: Resolving concurrent updates
heading: Alternatives#
text: Distributed data types provide defined merge behaviour for supported structures. Conditional updates can reduce ordinary races, but their boundaries still matter. Turning off sibling retention changes how competing content is discarded; it does not make the underlying operations transactional.

title: How distributed queries execute
text: The Query API distributes index work across the vnodes covering the requested bucket. Each vnode scans its local index range, evaluates and filters terms, and contributes results to the requested accumulation.

title: How distributed queries execute
heading: The query pipeline#
text: The range selects candidate index entries. An evaluation expression extracts projected attributes from each term. A filter expression decides which candidates match.

title: How distributed queries execute
heading: The query pipeline#
text: An evaluation expression extracts projected attributes from each term. A filter expression decides which candidates match. Accumulation determines whether the result contains keys, terms, counts, or grouped values.

title: How distributed queries execute
heading: The query pipeline#
text: A filter expression decides which candidates match. Accumulation determines whether the result contains keys, terms, counts, or grouped values. Combination queries run multiple scans and combine their matches with set operations.

title: How distributed queries execute
heading: The query pipeline#
text: Accumulation determines whether the result contains keys, terms, counts, or grouped values. Combination queries run multiple scans and combine their matches with set operations. Performing those operations close to the partition avoids sending every intermediate result to one cluster-wide coordinator.

title: How distributed queries execute
heading: Parallelism and limits#
text: Partitions can work in parallel, but the response still depends on the participating work completing. A slow backend, broad range, expensive expression, or large result can dominate the request. Adding client concurrency can increase queueing rather than reduce the cost of an individual query.

title: How distributed queries execute
heading: Results are an interface choice#
text: Choose an accumulation method that yields exactly the information the application requires. Performing the count within the query avoids transferring a large key set solely for client‑side counting. Delivery of results, continuation semantics, and any release‑specific asynchronous behaviour are independent API responsibilities.

title: Query consistency and snapshots
text: A distributed query observes partition-local snapshots, not one transactionally consistent instant across the cluster. Concurrent object changes can therefore affect what the overall result represents.

title: Query consistency and snapshots
heading: A snapshot within a vnode#
text: Combination queries use one snapshot per vnode for their constituent scans. This keeps the local set operations consistent for a potential key within that vnode’s work. Other vnodes can take their snapshots at different times.

title: Query consistency and snapshots
heading: Changes across the cluster#
text: If an application updates related objects on different partitions, a query may see one change before another. There is no cross-object transaction connecting those changes. Inter-cluster replication introduces further timing differences between the datasets queried at each destination.

title: Query consistency and snapshots
heading: Retrieving objects after a query#
text: An index query returns discovery results. A later object fetch is another request and can encounter an updated value, siblings, or a missing object. Applications should tolerate that gap rather than treating a returned key as a reservation on the value.

title: Query consistency and snapshots
heading: Repeated and continued queries#
text: Use the API’s continuation contract for a larger result set. Do not assume that restarting the same query or using an unrelated request reproduces the original snapshot. For an audit requiring a stable dataset, control writes and define the observation window explicitly.

title: Query cost and result delivery
text: Query cost depends on how many index entries are examined, what work is done per entry, and how much data is returned. A small result does not necessarily mean a cheap query.

title: Query cost and result delivery
heading: Scanning and filtering#
text: A narrow ordered range reduces the candidates scanned. A selective filter applied after a broad scan can return few matches while still visiting many entries. Projected attributes can save object fetches, but they increase index size and evaluation work.

title: Query cost and result delivery
heading: Accumulation and transport#
text: Returning counts or grouped counts can reduce response size. Returning every key or term consumes more memory, network capacity, and client processing. Duplicate handling also changes the required work and the meaning of a count.

title: Query cost and result delivery
heading: Accumulation and transport#
text: Returning every key or term consumes more memory, network capacity, and client processing. Duplicate handling also changes the required work and the meaning of a count. Pagination bounds the amount delivered per response; it should not be assumed to eliminate the cost of the underlying search.

title: Query cost and result delivery
heading: Accumulation and transport#
text: Duplicate handling also changes the required work and the meaning of a count. Pagination bounds the amount delivered per response; it should not be assumed to eliminate the cost of the underlying search. Where a release supports queued delivery, disk-backed results change how consumers retrieve work and introduce queue lifecycle and completion requirements.

title: Query cost and result delivery
heading: Shared resources#
text: Queries compete with writes, compaction, repair, and other queries. It is recommended to measure tail latency and background progress as well as one isolated query’s elapsed time. A useful performance experiment would change one range, projection, filter, or accumulation choice and check that the answer remains correct.

title: Secondary indexes and projected attributes
text: Secondary indexes associate ordered terms with object keys. A query searches those terms to discover keys; it need not read and decode every object’s value first.

title: Secondary indexes and projected attributes
heading: Index design follows the question#
text: Choose an index term whose ordering makes the desired range small. For example, a people directory may sort an index by a location or name prefix. The application is responsible for writing index metadata consistently with the object content.

title: Secondary indexes and projected attributes
heading: Projected attributes#
text: An index term can include attributes needed for filtering or reporting. The Query API evaluates the term to extract those attributes, then applies a filter expression. This can avoid fetching full objects just to reject them, at the cost of larger terms and additional index work on writes.

title: Secondary indexes and projected attributes
heading: Projected attributes#
text: The Query API evaluates the term to extract those attributes, then applies a filter expression. This can avoid fetching full objects just to reject them, at the cost of larger terms and additional index work on writes. An attribute projected into an index is not automatically kept current by a relational schema.

title: Secondary indexes and projected attributes
heading: Projected attributes#
text: This can avoid fetching full objects just to reject them, at the cost of larger terms and additional index work on writes. An attribute projected into an index is not automatically kept current by a relational schema. Updating the underlying value must include the corresponding index changes.

title: Secondary indexes and projected attributes
heading: Backend and consistency boundaries#
text: Index capability depends on the selected backend. Distributed queries examine partition-local state; an index result is not a cluster-wide transactional snapshot. Fetching a returned key later can observe another version or a deletion.

title: Secondary indexes and projected attributes
heading: Backend and consistency boundaries#
text: Distributed queries examine partition-local state; an index result is not a cluster-wide transactional snapshot. Fetching a returned key later can observe another version or a deletion. You should use direct key lookup when the key is already known.

title: Secondary indexes and projected attributes
heading: Backend and consistency boundaries#
text: Fetching a returned key later can observe another version or a deletion. You should use direct key lookup when the key is already known. For discovery, verify the index against known records and measure the size of the range scanned, not only the number of returned matches.

title: From Dynamo and Riak to OpenRiak
text: OpenRiak continues the Riak family of distributed key/value databases. Its architecture carries forward Dynamo’s partitioning, replication, and application-visible treatment of concurrent updates, while adding Riak and OpenRiak implementations of those ideas.

title: From Dynamo and Riak to OpenRiak
heading: From a design to an implementation#
text: Dynamo describes a design for a highly available distributed store. Riak applied related principles using Erlang processes, a partitioned ring, configurable request acknowledgements, and pluggable local storage. A Dynamo concept is useful background, but it is not a specification of an OpenRiak command, setting, or failure guarantee.

title: From Dynamo and Riak to OpenRiak
heading: OpenRiak today#
text: OpenRiak develops the Riak codebase with current storage, anti-entropy, replication, and query capabilities. Leveled and TicTac anti-entropy are central to the newer storage and repair paths. Next-generation replication uses sources, queues, and sinks; older documentation about `riak_repl` describes a different, older replication implementation.

title: From Dynamo and Riak to OpenRiak
heading: Reading older material#
text: Historical Riak examples can help explain the design, but package names, runtime compatibility, backend recommendations, and operational interfaces must be checked for the installed release. The compatibility reference separates current, legacy, and experimental features. For the original design, see Dynamo: Amazon’s Highly Available Key-value Store.

title: What OpenRiak KV is
text: OpenRiak KV stores values under keys and distributes copies across a cluster of servers. An application supplies a bucket and key to write or retrieve an object; OpenRiak locates the responsible partitions and coordinates the request.

title: What OpenRiak KV is
heading: A distributed key/value store#
text: A key/value store works much like a massive distributed Dictionary: you provide a key, and the system returns the value associated with that key. A value can be any byte sequence—JSON, text, an image, or arbitrary binary data. The application defines what the data means, how keys are chosen, and how conflicting updates are resolved.

title: What OpenRiak KV is
heading: A distributed key/value store#
text: A value can be any byte sequence—JSON, text, an image, or arbitrary binary data. The application defines what the data means, how keys are chosen, and how conflicting updates are resolved. Nodes share responsibility for the keyspace.

title: What OpenRiak KV is
heading: A distributed key/value store#
text: The application defines what the data means, how keys are chosen, and how conflicting updates are resolved. Nodes share responsibility for the keyspace. Replicas allow a request to continue when some servers are unavailable, provided the request’s acknowledgement requirements can still be met.

title: What OpenRiak KV is
heading: A distributed key/value store#
text: Nodes share responsibility for the keyspace. Replicas allow a request to continue when some servers are unavailable, provided the request’s acknowledgement requirements can still be met. Reaching a single node is not by itself a guarantee that a read or write will succeed.

title: What OpenRiak KV is
heading: The application contract#
text: OpenRiak’s ordinary object operations are eventually consistent. Applications preserve causal context when updating an object and handle concurrent values when the bucket policy allows them. Distributed data types provide merge rules for supported counters and collections.

title: What OpenRiak KV is
heading: The application contract#
text: Applications preserve causal context when updating an object and handle concurrent values when the bucket policy allows them. Distributed data types provide merge rules for supported counters and collections. Key lookup is the basic access path.

title: What OpenRiak KV is
heading: The application contract#
text: Distributed data types provide merge rules for supported counters and collections. Key lookup is the basic access path. Secondary indexes and the Query API add indexed discovery when the selected backend supports them.

title: What OpenRiak KV is
heading: The application contract#
text: Key lookup is the basic access path. Secondary indexes and the Query API add indexed discovery when the selected backend supports them. They do not turn the database into a relational system with cross-object transactions.

title: Where OpenRiak fits
text: OpenRiak fits applications that can model their data as independently addressable objects and make explicit choices about availability, acknowledgement, and concurrent updates.

title: Where OpenRiak fits
heading: Workloads with natural keys#
text: User preferences, device state, catalog records, and event-derived views often have stable identifiers. A request can find one object directly without coordinating a join across many records. Separate buckets or bucket types let an application apply different policies to distinct datasets.

title: Where OpenRiak fits
heading: Workloads with natural keys#
text: A request can find one object directly without coordinating a join across many records. Separate buckets or bucket types let an application apply different policies to distinct datasets. The fit depends on update semantics as much as on scale.

title: Where OpenRiak fits
heading: Workloads with natural keys#
text: Separate buckets or bucket types let an application apply different policies to distinct datasets. The fit depends on update semantics as much as on scale. A preference record may tolerate a merge of concurrent edits.

title: Where OpenRiak fits
heading: Workloads with natural keys#
text: The fit depends on update semantics as much as on scale. A preference record may tolerate a merge of concurrent edits. A monetary transfer requiring an atomic change to two accounts needs a transaction mechanism outside ordinary OpenRiak object operations.

title: Where OpenRiak fits
heading: Availability has application consequences#
text: Accepting work during failures can leave replicas temporarily different. The application must decide whether to retry, reconcile siblings, use a mergeable data type, or reject an operation whose prerequisites cannot be met. More acknowledgements can improve a request’s resilience but do not create a cross-object transaction.

title: Where OpenRiak fits
heading: Access patterns determine the design#
text: Design keys for direct lookups and indexes for specific discovery queries. Large scans, unbounded result sets, and frequent rewriting of large objects have different costs from small keyed requests. Measure a representative workload, including repair and node loss, before committing to a deployment size.

title: Multi-cluster topologies and behaviour
text: A multi-cluster topology defines where writes originate, which clusters receive them, and how applications behave when a site or connection fails.

title: Multi-cluster topologies and behaviour
heading: One-way and bidirectional paths#
text: A one-way path is suitable when one cluster owns writes and another receives a copy. Bidirectional paths allow both clusters to originate changes, but do not supply a global transaction order. Concurrent updates made at different sites still require compatible object policies and conflict handling.

title: Multi-cluster topologies and behaviour
heading: Cascades and selective replication#
text: A cascade forwards changes through an intermediate cluster. It can reduce direct connectivity, but the intermediate site becomes part of the delivery and recovery path. Filters and forwarding behaviour determine which changes continue beyond it; a diagram alone does not establish that every write reaches every destination.

title: Multi-cluster topologies and behaviour
heading: Cascades and selective replication#
text: It can reduce direct connectivity, but the intermediate site becomes part of the delivery and recovery path. Filters and forwarding behaviour determine which changes continue beyond it; a diagram alone does not establish that every write reaches every destination. Bucket selection and queue definitions can restrict a path to a dataset.

title: Multi-cluster topologies and behaviour
heading: Cascades and selective replication#
text: Filters and forwarding behaviour determine which changes continue beyond it; a diagram alone does not establish that every write reaches every destination. Bucket selection and queue definitions can restrict a path to a dataset. Keep that scope consistent with reconciliation and with the application’s assumptions about where data exists.

title: Multi-cluster topologies and behaviour
heading: Failure and recovery#
text: Failover requires an application routing decision as well as replicated data. Measure replication lag and define what data loss or stale reads are acceptable before switching traffic. When the original site returns, reconcile it before assuming it is an equivalent destination.

title: Multi-cluster topologies and behaviour
heading: Failure and recovery#
text: Measure replication lag and define what data loss or stale reads are acceptable before switching traffic. When the original site returns, reconcile it before assuming it is an equivalent destination. Cross-cluster replication also replicates unwanted logical changes.

title: Multi-cluster topologies and behaviour
heading: Failure and recovery#
text: When the original site returns, reconcile it before assuming it is an equivalent destination. Cross-cluster replication also replicates unwanted logical changes. Independent, recoverable backups remain a separate concern.

title: Read repair and TicTac anti-entropy
text: Read repair and TicTac active anti-entropy both help replicas converge. Read repair reacts to replica differences found while serving a read; TicTac compares replica state independently of client reads.

title: Read repair and TicTac anti-entropy
heading: Finding differences efficiently#
text: TicTac uses trees summarising keys and version information. Matching summaries can establish that the compared scope agrees without exchanging every object. A mismatch narrows the search to branches, segments, and eventually keys whose versions need comparison.

title: Read repair and TicTac anti-entropy
heading: Finding differences efficiently#
text: Matching summaries can establish that the compared scope agrees without exchanging every object. A mismatch narrows the search to branches, segments, and eventually keys whose versions need comparison. Repairing a difference costs more than confirming agreement: it requires locating versions and transferring objects.

title: Read repair and TicTac anti-entropy
heading: Finding differences efficiently#
text: A mismatch narrows the search to branches, segments, and eventually keys whose versions need comparison. Repairing a difference costs more than confirming agreement: it requires locating versions and transferring objects. Throttling and worker limits balance convergence against the resources needed by application traffic.

title: Read repair and TicTac anti-entropy
heading: Trees and stores#
text: Cached summaries must themselves remain consistent with stored data. Rebuilds and targeted refreshes correct stale tree state. Backend integration determines whether anti-entropy can use a native store or needs a parallel store, with different storage and rebuild costs.

title: Read repair and TicTac anti-entropy
heading: Limits of repair#
text: Repair can copy surviving data and reconcile known versions. It cannot reconstruct a value when every usable copy and backup has been lost. Nor does it decide an application’s business meaning when two updates are concurrent.

title: Read repair and TicTac anti-entropy
heading: Limits of repair#
text: It cannot reconstruct a value when every usable copy and backup has been lost. Nor does it decide an application’s business meaning when two updates are concurrent. Inter-cluster reconciliation uses related comparison principles but compares cluster-wide coverage rather than assuming identical vnode layouts.

title: Read repair and TicTac anti-entropy
heading: Limits of repair#
text: Nor does it decide an application’s business meaning when two updates are concurrent. Inter-cluster reconciliation uses related comparison principles but compares cluster-wide coverage rather than assuming identical vnode layouts. Legacy active anti-entropy is a separate implementation with different settings.

title: Real-time replication and fullsync
text: Real-time replication delivers ongoing changes, while fullsync compares datasets and repairs differences. A healthy multi-cluster deployment needs an understood path for both ordinary delivery and recovery after interruptions.

title: Real-time replication and fullsync
heading: The fast path#
text: New changes enter the source queue and are consumed by the destination. This reduces the delay between a write and its arrival at the other cluster, but delivery is asynchronous. Client success at the source is not a transaction committed simultaneously in both clusters.

title: Real-time replication and fullsync
heading: Reconciliation#
text: Fullsync compares version information for a selected dataset and identifies objects needing transfer. It can recover differences after queue loss, a long outage, or initial seeding. Its duration depends on the comparison scope, amount of divergence, transfer capacity, and repair controls.

title: Real-time replication and fullsync
heading: Reconciliation#
text: It can recover differences after queue loss, a long outage, or initial seeding. Its duration depends on the comparison scope, amount of divergence, transfer capacity, and repair controls. Completion should be assessed through the exchange result and subsequent checks, not simply through an empty real-time queue.

title: Real-time replication and fullsync
heading: Reconciliation#
text: Its duration depends on the comparison scope, amount of divergence, transfer capacity, and repair controls. Completion should be assessed through the exchange result and subsequent checks, not simply through an empty real-time queue. Concurrent writes can continue creating new differences while a comparison runs.

title: Real-time replication and fullsync
heading: Replication generations#
text: For next-generation replication, use TicTac-based reconciliation and the current source/sink controls. Older instructions about a legacy AAE fullsync strategy, identical ring sizes, or `riak_repl` settings apply to their documented generation. They are not prerequisites to copy into a current deployment without checking applicability.

title: Replication generations and compatibility
text: OpenRiak documentation covers more than one replication implementation. Next-generation replication, legacy v3 replication, and legacy v2 replication must be identified explicitly when configuring or diagnosing a deployment.

title: Replication generations and compatibility
heading: Next-generation replication#
text: The current source/queue/sink design uses its own queue, consumer, and reconciliation controls. Its TicTac-based comparisons do not imply that legacy replication settings or transports are interchangeable.

title: Replication generations and compatibility
heading: Legacy Replication#
text: Legacy v2 and v3 belong to the `riak_repl` family. They have their own listeners, connection establishment, fullsync mechanisms, and compatibility requirements. A command containing the word “fullsync” is not sufficient to identify which implementation it controls.

title: Replication generations and compatibility
heading: Migration boundaries#
text: Changing generation is a data-movement and cutover exercise. You should always check compatibility, data policies, existing filters, conflict handling, and the route used for deletions. Verify convergence before switching applications, and retain a recovery pathway while both systems can still be compared.

title: Replication sources, queues, and sinks
text: Next-generation replication moves objects from a source cluster through named queues to consumers in a sink cluster. Each connection has a direction; reverse replication is a separate path.

title: Replication sources, queues, and sinks
heading: Sources and queues#
text: A source selects eligible changes and offers them through a queue. Queue definitions and filters determine which dataset a consumer sees. The queue can carry references or object information according to the implementation and configuration; the sink must use the matching interface.

title: Replication sources, queues, and sinks
heading: Sources and queues#
text: Queue definitions and filters determine which dataset a consumer sees. The queue can carry references or object information according to the implementation and configuration; the sink must use the matching interface. Queues decouple incoming writes from downstream processing, but they are bounded resources.

title: Replication sources, queues, and sinks
heading: Sources and queues#
text: The queue can carry references or object information according to the implementation and configuration; the sink must use the matching interface. Queues decouple incoming writes from downstream processing, but they are bounded resources. A destination that is unavailable or slower than the source can accumulate lag.

title: Replication sources, queues, and sinks
heading: Sources and queues#
text: Queues decouple incoming writes from downstream processing, but they are bounded resources. A destination that is unavailable or slower than the source can accumulate lag. A empty queue alone does not prove that two complete datasets agree.

title: Replication sources, queues, and sinks
heading: Sink consumers#
text: Sink workers fetch queued work and apply it to local replicas. Their throughput depends on network transfer, source service, sink writes, and competition with other work. More consumers can help a constrained pipeline only while the underlying resources can handle them.

title: Replication sources, queues, and sinks
heading: Recovery#
text: Real-time delivery carries ongoing changes. Reconciliation checks for differences that are not represented by currently queued work, including interruptions and historical divergence. Treat queue monitoring and dataset comparison as complementary checks.

title: Replication sources, queues, and sinks
heading: Recovery#
text: Reconciliation checks for differences that are not represented by currently queued work, including interruptions and historical divergence. Treat queue monitoring and dataset comparison as complementary checks. The source/sink path is independent of the legacy `riak_repl` connection model; do not mix their runtime controls.

title: Targeted reconciliation and AAE folds
text: Targeted reconciliation limits inspection or repair to the data relevant to a question. AAE folds can examine bucket, key-range, time, segment, or object characteristics without requiring an unbounded client-side key listing.

title: Targeted reconciliation and AAE folds
heading: Choose the scope of the incident#
text: If a replication interruption affects one dataset and time window, that scope can guide a re-replication operation. If a diagnostic question concerns oversized objects, a fold can identify candidates before the application fetches their full contents. Filters describe a selection, not proof that every relevant event lies inside it.

title: Targeted reconciliation and AAE folds
heading: Choose the scope of the incident#
text: If a diagnostic question concerns oversized objects, a fold can identify candidates before the application fetches their full contents. Filters describe a selection, not proof that every relevant event lies inside it. Modification-time windows, for example, depend on the meaning of the stored modification data.

title: Targeted reconciliation and AAE folds
heading: Choose the scope of the incident#
text: Filters describe a selection, not proof that every relevant event lies inside it. Modification-time windows, for example, depend on the meaning of the stored modification data. Validate boundaries and include the recovery history when selecting them.

title: Targeted reconciliation and AAE folds
heading: Inspection and mutation differ#
text: Listing, counting, and statistics observe data. Repair, erasure, reaping, and re-replication can change state or schedule substantial work. Preview candidates and check completion using the operation’s actual contract.

title: Targeted reconciliation and AAE folds
heading: Cost and progress#
text: A narrow result does not always imply a narrow backend scan. Folds use cluster coverage and available backend filtering, and compete for workers and storage resources. A timeout at the requesting console is not necessarily proof that background work stopped.

title: Targeted reconciliation and AAE folds
heading: Cost and progress#
text: Folds use cluster coverage and available backend filtering, and compete for workers and storage resources. A timeout at the requesting console is not necessarily proof that background work stopped. TicTac’s cached comparisons and bounded folds complement each other: one detects broad disagreement efficiently, and the other inspects or acts on a selected scope.

title: Identities, authentication, and permissions
text: A user identifies a client, an authentication source selects how a connection proves that identity, and permissions determine which operations it can perform. Groups allow related users to share permission assignments.

title: Identities, authentication, and permissions
heading: Authentication sources#
text: A source rule connects a user or group and network origin with an authentication method. Credentials alone are not sufficient if the connection does not match an appropriate source rule. Conversely, a broad rule can admit connections from more places than intended.

title: Identities, authentication, and permissions
heading: Permissions and scope#
text: Grants associate supported operations with users or groups and a resource scope. Scope matters: permission for one bucket is not necessarily permission for another namespace. Group membership changes can alter several effective grants at once.

title: Identities, authentication, and permissions
heading: Identity lifecycle#
text: Applications need a way to rotate credentials, remove departed identities, and check the resulting permissions. Sharing one unrestricted user makes those changes harder to isolate and obscures which application needs which access.

title: Identities, authentication, and permissions
heading: A useful verification model#
text: For each role, you should test an allowed operation and a deliberately denied operation against the intended endpoint and namespace. Also test a connection from an unapproved origin. These checks distinguish successful authentication from correct authorization.

title: Security boundaries and trust
text: OpenRiak security separates client authentication and permissions from trust in the host, cluster network, and administrative environment. Each exposed interface needs a deliberate access boundary.

title: Security boundaries and trust
heading: Client access#
text: Authentication establishes an identity; authorization controls the operations that identity may perform. Protecting the transport with TLS addresses another question: whether peers can establish trust and whether traffic is protected in transit.

title: Security boundaries and trust
heading: Administrative access#
text: Access to the service account, node configuration, or an Erlang console can expose much broader control than an application’s bucket permissions. Treat node-to-node connectivity and Erlang distribution credentials as cluster administration capabilities.

title: Security boundaries and trust
heading: Network boundaries#
text: Bind and filter interfaces according to the intended clients and peers. A secure application listener does not automatically protect another listener, replication endpoint, or operating-system login path. Include load balancers and intermediate systems in the trust model.

title: Security boundaries and trust
heading: Failure behaviour#
text: You should test rejected access requests as well as successful access requests. A configuration that lets the intended application connect may still admit a wider source range or permission set than intended. Administrative recovery access should be planned before changing authentication or certificates.

title: TLS and certificate trust
text: TLS protects a connection only when the client and server use an appropriate trust chain and verify the peer they intended to reach. Encryption without identity verification leaves an important part of that contract unmet.

title: TLS and certificate trust
heading: Certificates and trust#
text: A certificate binds an identity to a public key. A trust store identifies the issuers a peer accepts. The private key must remain available to its service and protected from unrelated users.

title: TLS and certificate trust
heading: Certificates and trust#
text: A trust store identifies the issuers a peer accepts. The private key must remain available to its service and protected from unrelated users. Endpoint names, certificate names, validity periods, and chains must agree with the actual connection.

title: TLS and certificate trust
heading: TLS and application permissions#
text: A trusted transport does not itself grant access to every bucket. Authentication and authorization still apply according to the configured method and interface. Client-certificate authentication also requires a deliberate mapping from the verified certificate to an accepted identity.

title: TLS and certificate trust
heading: Rotation#
text: Rotation changes the trust material while connections and applications may still use the old material. An overlap period can allow clients to accept the new chain before the old one is removed. The sequence depends on the listener, client library, and authentication method.

title: TLS and certificate trust
heading: Rotation#
text: An overlap period can allow clients to accept the new chain before the old one is removed. The sequence depends on the listener, client library, and authentication method. Verify both trusted and untrusted connections after a change, and test name verification rather than suppressing it to make a connection succeed.

title: Capacity and growth
text: Cluster capacity must cover live data, replicated copies, indexes, retained history, and the temporary work needed to grow or recover. Steady-state disk occupancy alone is an incomplete sizing measure.

title: Capacity and growth
heading: What consumes resources#
text: Object count and key size affect per-key metadata. Value size affects transfer and storage. Index terms add write and query work.

title: Capacity and growth
heading: What consumes resources#
text: Value size affects transfer and storage. Index terms add write and query work. Siblings, tombstones, and obsolete backend records can make stored data larger than the application’s current logical dataset.

title: Capacity and growth
heading: What consumes resources#
text: Index terms add write and query work. Siblings, tombstones, and obsolete backend records can make stored data larger than the application’s current logical dataset. Memory needs depend on the backend as well as on caches, concurrent requests, and background processes.

title: Capacity and growth
heading: What consumes resources#
text: Siblings, tombstones, and obsolete backend records can make stored data larger than the application’s current logical dataset. Memory needs depend on the backend as well as on caches, concurrent requests, and background processes. CPU and network needs depend on access patterns, replication, and repair, not only on stored bytes.

title: Capacity and growth
heading: Headroom is part of usable capacity#
text: When a node fails, survivors must absorb work and help restore redundancy. Membership changes also move partitions and can temporarily retain both old and new copies. A cluster that fits only when every node is healthy cannot necessarily complete its own recovery.

title: Capacity and growth
heading: Growth over time#
text: It is recommended that you measure distributions as well as averages: hot keys, uneven bucket sizes, and a few large objects can concentrate work. This can be used to forecast growth to the next expansion window, then test that expansion and a representative failure while application traffic continues.

title: How Bitcask stores data
text: Bitcask stores values in append-only data files and keeps an in-memory directory locating the current record for each key. A lookup uses that directory to find the corresponding value on disk.

title: How Bitcask stores data
heading: Writes and obsolete records#
text: Updating an object appends a new record. Older records remain physically present until a merge rewrites the live data and removes eligible obsolete files. Deleting visible objects therefore does not immediately return all of their disk space.

title: How Bitcask stores data
heading: Memory follows the keyspace#
text: The key directory has an entry for each retained key. Small values do not eliminate that per-key cost, so a workload with many tiny objects can become memory-bound even when the value files are modest. Startup also needs to reconstruct the directory using the stored files and hints.

title: How Bitcask stores data
heading: Persistence and merging#
text: The write path and configured synchronisation behaviours determine if acknowledged work is resilient to process or host failure. A merge consumes I/O and temporary capacity alongside foreground traffic. Scheduling merges changes when that cost is paid; it does not make obsolete records disappear for free.

title: How Bitcask stores data
heading: Persistence and merging#
text: A merge consumes I/O and temporary capacity alongside foreground traffic. Scheduling merges changes when that cost is paid; it does not make obsolete records disappear for free. This does allow you to reduce the impact of these merges on regular operations however.

title: How Bitcask stores data
heading: Persistence and merging#
text: Scheduling merges changes when that cost is paid; it does not make obsolete records disappear for free. This does allow you to reduce the impact of these merges on regular operations however. Bitcask’s key/value design should not be assumed to provide the same secondary-index capabilities as Leveled.

title: How Bitcask stores data
heading: Persistence and merging#
text: This does allow you to reduce the impact of these merges on regular operations however. Bitcask’s key/value design should not be assumed to provide the same secondary-index capabilities as Leveled. Choose an engine from the access pattern rather than from a throughput figure measured on another workload.

title: How Leveled stores data
text: Leveled separates the journal of stored values from the ledger used to locate current objects and index entries. This supports indexed access without keeping the complete key directory in memory.

title: How Leveled stores data
heading: Journal and ledger#
text: The journal records object values. The Ledger structures describe keys, metadata, and indexes and are organised so that reads can locate the needed state efficiently. Caches are used to reduce repeated work, while durable files let the store recover state across restarts.

title: How Leveled stores data
heading: Snapshots and background work#
text: Snapshots let a query or fold examine a stable local view while other work proceeds. They are local storage views, not an all encompassing view of all vnodes. Holding old views can also delay reclamation of files still needed by readers.

title: How Leveled stores data
heading: Snapshots and background work#
text: They are local storage views, not an all encompassing view of all vnodes. Holding old views can also delay reclamation of files still needed by readers. Compaction reorganises stored structures and removes eligible obsolete state.

title: How Leveled stores data
heading: Snapshots and background work#
text: Holding old views can also delay reclamation of files still needed by readers. Compaction reorganises stored structures and removes eligible obsolete state. It consumes disk bandwidth and spare space.

title: How Leveled stores data
heading: Snapshots and background work#
text: Compaction reorganises stored structures and removes eligible obsolete state. It consumes disk bandwidth and spare space. Increasing foreground throughput without allowing this work to keep up can transfer the cost into later latency or storage pressure.

title: How Leveled stores data
heading: Recovery and maintenance#
text: Journal, ledger, and backup artefacts have different roles. Removing a file solely because it looks old can remove a state needed by an active store or recovery procedure. Use the backend-specific backup, cleanup, and rebuild guidance within this documentation, and verify indexes as well as object reads after a recovery to ensure a smooth recovery experience.

title: Latency, queues, and resource contention
text: Latency is the time a request waits as well as the time spent doing its work. Once a shared resource approaches saturation, queues can grow even when the operation itself has not changed.

title: Latency, queues, and resource contention
heading: Shared resources#
text: Foreground requests compete with compaction, queries, handoffs, replication, and repair for CPU, memory, disk, and network capacity. Erlang processes provide concurrency, but they still run on finite schedulers and physical resources.

title: Latency, queues, and resource contention
heading: Follow the queue#
text: A slow client response may reflect a backend queue, a busy worker pool, a delayed replica, network transfer, or scheduling pressure. A single average latency cannot distinguish these cases. Compare tail latency, queue length, resource utilisation, and background progress over the same interval.

title: Latency, queues, and resource contention
heading: Throughput and concurrency#
text: Increasing concurrency can improve utilisation when resources are idle. Beyond saturation, it adds waiting and memory pressure. Raising timeouts can hide a symptom while leaving the queue to grow; raising worker counts can move the bottleneck to storage.

title: Latency, queues, and resource contention
heading: Testing throughput and resource usage#
text: In testing it is recommended to change one measured constraint at a time and keep a comparable workload. Confirm that the change improves the application’s target latency or throughput while repair and maintenance continue to complete. A benchmark that pauses all background work describes a different operating condition.

title: Multiple backends and prefix routing
text: Multi-backend routing assigns different datasets to different local storage engines. A routing layer selects the backend; it does not combine their files into one interchangeable format.

title: Multiple backends and prefix routing
heading: Policy-based routing#
text: Different buckets can have different storage requirements. A routing configuration can associate data with named backend definitions, each with its own settings and resource use. Prefix routing selects an engine using the configured prefix rules.

title: Multiple backends and prefix routing
heading: Why a route change is significant#
text: Existing objects remain in the engine that stored them. Changing the selection rule can direct future requests elsewhere without migrating those objects, making data appear missing or separating newer writes from older state. A migration therefore needs an explicit inventory, copy or replacement procedure, and verification.

title: Multiple backends and prefix routing
heading: Why a route change is significant#
text: Changing the selection rule can direct future requests elsewhere without migrating those objects, making data appear missing or separating newer writes from older state. A migration therefore needs an explicit inventory, copy or replacement procedure, and verification. Switching back a route is not a universal rollback once writes have reached the new destination.

title: Multiple backends and prefix routing
heading: Operational cost#
text: Multiple engines share node memory, file descriptors, storage bandwidth, and recovery time. Each also brings its own compaction, persistence, and backup behaviour. A mixed deployment must account for the total resource use and for feature restrictions in each route.

title: Multiple backends and prefix routing
heading: Operational cost#
text: Each also brings its own compaction, persistence, and backup behaviour. A mixed deployment must account for the total resource use and for feature restrictions in each route. Use the version specific legacy and specialist reference to check the availability and limitations of the particular routing implementation.

title: Persistence, filesystems, and space reclamation
text: Persistence concerns which acknowledged data survives a failure. Space reclamation concerns when storage occupied by obsolete state can be reused. Both depend on the backend and filesystem, but they answer different questions.

title: Persistence, filesystems, and space reclamation
heading: From memory to durable storage#
text: A write can pass through process memory, operating-system caches, and storage-controller caches before reaching stable media. Backend synchronisation settings and request acknowledgement options determine which steps a success response relies on. Replication adds copies, but shared power or storage failures can still affect several copies together.

title: Persistence, filesystems, and space reclamation
heading: Logical and physical deletion#
text: An update or tombstone can make older records obsolete without immediately removing their bytes. Bitcask merges and Leveled compaction reclaim eligible space later. Snapshots, retained versions, and active work can keep files necessary after a newer logical state exists.

title: Persistence, filesystems, and space reclamation
heading: Filesystem effects#
text: Capacity planning should include temporary files and background rewriting, not just the sum of current values. Latency spikes can reflect I/O contention or storage limits even while the application request rate is unchanged. Erlang garbage collection reclaims process memory.

title: Persistence, filesystems, and space reclamation
heading: Filesystem effects#
text: Latency spikes can reflect I/O contention or storage limits even while the application request rate is unchanged. Erlang garbage collection reclaims process memory. It is not the mechanism that compacts database files or reaps replicated tombstones.

title: Storage backend trade-offs
text: A storage backend manages each vnode’s local data. Its design determines memory use, persistence behaviour, index support, and the maintenance work that competes with requests.

title: Storage backend trade-offs
heading: Bitcask and Leveled#
text: Bitcask appends values to data files and keeps a key directory in memory. Its fit depends on the size of the keyspace and available memory. It is a natural option for direct key/value access when that directory can be accommodated.

title: Storage backend trade-offs
heading: Bitcask and Leveled#
text: Its fit depends on the size of the keyspace and available memory. It is a natural option for direct key/value access when that directory can be accommodated. Leveled separates journaled values from indexed state and supports workloads requiring secondary indexes.

title: Storage backend trade-offs
heading: Bitcask and Leveled#
text: It is a natural option for direct key/value access when that directory can be accommodated. Leveled separates journaled values from indexed state and supports workloads requiring secondary indexes. Caches, compaction, and snapshots affect its resource use and operational behaviour.

title: Storage backend trade-offs
heading: Other backend names#
text: LevelDB, the memory backend, and multi-backend routing appear in historical and specialist deployments. Their presence in the configuration schema does not make them equivalent choices for a new deployment. The release-specific capability and feature-status references describe applicability.

title: Storage backend trade-offs
heading: A choice persists with the data#
text: Changing a backend setting does not convert existing backend files. Migration must preserve objects, metadata, indexes, and the required recovery path. You should benchmark the intended workload and include startup, compaction, and replica recovery before selecting an engine.

title: Coordinate an update with a latch object
text: Use a small, purpose‑built object to mark when a specific task is in progress-like claiming a batch. Before you create that marker, spell out how ownership will be assigned and how any stopped or unfinished work will be recovered.

title: Coordinate an update with a latch object
heading: Establish the contract#
text: Pick a single key to represent each claim, and store both the owner and the work identifier in its value. Every writer that participates in the workflow must follow the same conditional‑update rules. Remember that a latch only protects the key it’s attached to—other keys are not updated atomically—so review the boundaries of conditional updates before depending on it.

title: Coordinate an update with a latch object
heading: Create the claim#
text: When using the HTTP object endpoint, send the creation request with `If-None-Match: *.` Include deliberate application data in the body. If the request fails its precondition, it means another value already holds the claim; treat this as a signal to stop, not as permission to overwrite the existing value.

title: Coordinate an update with a latch object
heading: Complete or recover the work#
text: Read the marker, keep its causal context, and confirm that the owner matches before moving the work forward. Make downstream steps safe to retry by using the work identifier. Because timeouts can leave a valid claim behind, always inspect the marker before attempting a retry.

title: Coordinate an update with a latch object
heading: Verify contention scenario#
text: Test how the system behaves when two workers try to claim the same identifier, when a worker stops immediately after claiming, and when a retry happens after an uncertain response. Ensure your recovery logic avoids repeating non‑idempotent actions and doesn’t leave any work permanently unclaimable. Preserve sibling‑handling logic for rare or exceptional concurrency cases.

title: Resolve concurrent object updates

title: Resolve concurrent object updates
heading: Apply the application’s merge rule#
text: You should merge values according to their meaning: preserve independent changes, combine collections where valid, or request user intervention for incompatible edits. A wall-clock timestamp alone is not a safe general conflict rule. See Resolving concurrent updates for the choices.

title: Resolve concurrent object updates

text: Send the resolved value with the context from the complete read, preserving required indexes and metadata. Read again and confirm that the resulting value matches the merge. Another concurrent update may create new siblings, so the resolution path must be repeatable and must not assume one attempt always finishes.

title: Store immutable data through the write-once path

title: Store immutable data through the write-once path

text: You should run an inventory of bucket types using the write-once property and verify that keys are truly immutable. Identify any reliance on indexes, conditional updates, replication, or repair before changing the policy. Use Write-once interface for the interface constraints.

title: Store immutable data through the write-once path

text: Create a separate test type using ordinary object properties, write representative immutable values through Create and store an object, and compare latency and required features. Preserve the application’s key uniqueness rule; the normal PUT path does not by itself prevent an accidental replacement.

title: Store immutable data through the write-once path

text: Move or replay the data into the intended type or cluster and validate known keys and counts. Update clients to the normal endpoint and policy, retaining the original data until verification is complete. Do not enable replication on an old write-once workload and assume previously uncoordinated writes have been delivered.

title: Update an object with causal context

Use Make conditional reads and writes when the operation should fail if the fetched version has changed, and handle that failure by refetching rather than blindly retrying the old request.

title: Recover a cluster after a widespread failure
text: Recover service after a widespread failure by first preserving evidence and determining which data copies remain trustworthy. Avoid making membership changes while the extent of the failure is still unknown.

title: Recover a cluster after a widespread failure
heading: Stabilise and inventory#
text: Stop automated destructive recovery actions and coordinate application writes where necessary. Record unavailable nodes, storage health, network failures, logs, and the last known healthy membership. Preserve affected disks and metadata before attempting repair.

title: Recover a cluster after a widespread failure
heading: Choose the recovery source#
text: If nodes retain intact data, restore connectivity and restart them with their original identities. If only selected members lost storage, use Repair a vnode or node from surviving replicas with verified surviving replicas. If local replicas are insufficient, evaluate another reconciled cluster or a verified backup.

title: Recover a cluster after a widespread failure
heading: Choose the recovery source#
text: If only selected members lost storage, use Repair a vnode or node from surviving replicas with verified surviving replicas. If local replicas are insufficient, evaluate another reconciled cluster or a verified backup. Current-generation replication uses the controls in Next-generation replication runtime controls, not legacy `riak_repl` commands.

title: Recover a cluster after a widespread failure
heading: Recover in a controlled environment#
text: Bring back the smallest well-understood set of intact members first, inspect their view of the ring, and expand recovery deliberately. For backup recovery, follow Restore node data from a backup in isolation. Do not force-remove multiple members simply to make membership output look clean; that can discard the information needed for recovery.

title: Recover a cluster after a widespread failure
heading: Prove readiness#
text: Check known critical keys, causal histories, indexes, bucket policies, security, and replication scope. Wait for the required repairs and reconciliation, then restore traffic gradually while monitoring errors and latency. Record any unrecoverable time range or data scope explicitly.

If a source fails mid-operation, reassess recovery rather than blindly continuing the rolling sequence.

title: Restore node data from a backup
text: Restore a verified backup into an isolated recovery environment before returning application traffic. For one failed member in an otherwise healthy cluster, prefer replica-based repair using Repair a vnode or node from surviving replicas.

title: Restore node data from a backup
heading: Verify the recovery set#
text: Check backup integrity, capture times, node identities, release and OTP versions, backend layout, and cluster metadata. Ensure the selected files cover the intended dataset. Isolate the recovery cluster from live peers and replication so old or new state cannot mix unexpectedly.

title: Restore node data from a backup
heading: Restore stopped nodes#
text: Install the matching software and stop all nodes being restored. Move existing backend directories aside rather than merging them with backup files. Restore data, ring and cluster metadata, configuration, and permissions to the recorded locations.

title: Restore node data from a backup
heading: Restore stopped nodes#
text: Move existing backend directories aside rather than merging them with backup files. Restore data, ring and cluster metadata, configuration, and permissions to the recorded locations. For a Leveled hot backup, restore the saved journal layout into the intended Leveled store.

title: Restore node data from a backup
heading: Restore stopped nodes#
text: Restore data, ring and cluster metadata, configuration, and permissions to the recorded locations. For a Leveled hot backup, restore the saved journal layout into the intended Leveled store. Its ledger is rebuilt at startup; do not reuse an unrelated ledger from a later state.

title: Restore node data from a backup
heading: Restore stopped nodes#
text: For a Leveled hot backup, restore the saved journal layout into the intended Leveled store. Its ledger is rebuilt at startup; do not reuse an unrelated ledger from a later state. Preserve the original backup while testing.

title: Restore node data from a backup
heading: Start and validate#
text: Start the isolated nodes, wait for ledger rebuilds and membership recovery, then inspect transfers and AAE. Compare a recorded sample of values, siblings, indexes, and bucket policies. Explain any writes newer than the backup that the recovery cannot contain.

title: Restore node data from a backup
heading: Return traffic deliberately#
text: Reconcile the recovered state with the intended live environment under an explicit plan, then restore client routing. Keep the displaced files until the recovery is verified. A successful process start alone is not evidence that the backup was complete.

title: Roll back a compatible cluster upgrade
text: Roll back a cluster upgrade only when the previous release can read the current data and metadata formats. There is no blanket guarantee that an arbitrary older package can safely open newer state.

title: Roll back a compatible cluster upgrade
heading: Establish a compatible rollback point#
text: Review source and target release notes, enabled features, backend formats, compression, and custom modules. Determine whether newer writes or metadata changes have crossed a compatibility boundary. If compatibility is uncertain, restore an isolated known-compatible backup or migrate through a tested path instead of opening live files with an older executable.

title: Roll back a compatible cluster upgrade
heading: Rehearse and select a pilot#
text: Test the rollback on a representative copy. Keep the previous package and its compatible configuration, and record which changes must be reversed. Preserve the current state before replacing the pilot node’s package.

title: Roll back a compatible cluster upgrade
heading: Roll back one member#
text: Drain and stop the pilot, install the verified earlier package, and restore the compatible configuration without mixing generated files from different releases. Start and inspect logs, reads, indexes, AAE, and replication. Wait for recovery before proceeding to another member.

title: Roll back a compatible cluster upgrade
heading: Verify the whole cluster#
text: Follow the same health gates as Perform a rolling restart. Confirm all members and connected clusters converge, and that clients no longer request target-only features. Stop the sequence and retain evidence if the older release cannot interpret the state.

title: Upgrade an OpenRiak KV cluster
text: Upgrade an existing cluster in a rehearsed rolling sequence, preserving data and configuration on every member. Read the exact source and target release notes before selecting a package.

text: Do not attempt a direct rolling upgrade from Riak 3.0 to OpenRiak KV 3.4.0 or 3.4.1. Breaking Erlang distribution compatibility prevents those nodes from sharing the required mixed-version cluster. A staged route through 3.2 requires checking and rehearsing the exact releases and OTP builds at each step.

title: Upgrade an OpenRiak KV cluster
heading: Upgrade a pilot member#

title: Repair inconsistent secondary indexes

title: Repair inconsistent secondary indexes

text: `riak admin repair-2i` is a legacy index-repair interface. Inspect its help and backend applicability before starting it; it is not a general Leveled index reconstruction command. If the application wrote incorrect index metadata, repair the application write path and rewrite affected objects with complete current index entries and preserved context.

title: Repair inconsistent secondary indexes
heading: Check the repair interface#
text: Inspect its help and backend applicability before starting it; it is not a general Leveled index reconstruction command. If the application wrote incorrect index metadata, repair the application write path and rewrite affected objects with complete current index entries and preserved context. If a Leveled store is damaged, use its documented store-repair procedure and preserve the original store first.

title: Repair inconsistent secondary indexes

text: Repeat the same known queries and compare fetched object metadata. Check range boundaries and multiple terms for one key. Monitor repair progress and foreground latency, and retain the candidate list and pre-repair observations until correctness is established.
