title: Run and retrieve a long-running AAE fold
heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `operation` Argument `list-buckets``find-keys``count-keys``find-tombstones``count-tombstones``reap-tombstones``object-stats``erase-keys``repair-keys` — Required Not repeatable Select the range operation. Use count variants before data-removal operations. `nval` Argument positive integer — Optional Not repeatable Replication factor for list-buckets, supplied as `nval=3`. `bucket` Argument bucket name or type/name — Optional Not repeatable Bucket as `bucket=name` or `bucket=type/name`. Required by bucket-range operations. `key_range` Argument `all`FROM,TO — Optional Not repeatable Use `key_range=all` or comma-separated lower and upper bounds. `modified_range` Argument `all`timestamp bounds — Optional Not repeatable Use `modified_range=all` or comma-separated RFC3339 timestamps.

title: Run and retrieve a long-running AAE fold
heading: Arguments and options
text: `segments` Argument `all`segment-list;tree-size — Optional Not repeatable Use `segments=all`, or a quoted segment list and tree size such as `segments=0,1;small`. `sibling_count` Argument non-negative integer — Optional Not repeatable Sibling-count threshold for key finding/counting. Supply this or object_size. `object_size` Argument non-negative integer — Optional Not repeatable Object-size threshold in bytes for key finding/counting. Supply this or sibling_count. `change_method` Argument `count``local``jobs:N` — Optional Not repeatable For destructive operations, start with `change_method=count`. The runtime also parses local and jobs:N; check the matching Erlang API before using a job mode.

title: Run and retrieve a long-running AAE fold
heading: Arguments and options
text: `--format` Option `csv``human``json` `human` Optional Not repeatable Select the Clique output writer. `human` is readable terminal output; `csv` renders tables only; `json` renders structured status records. The launcher can append an `ok` line, so complete stdout is not necessarily a standalone JSON document. An unknown writer warns and falls back to `human`. `--help` /`-h` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Print usage without executing the command. The short spelling is `-h`. `--outfile` /`-o` Option filesystem path — Optional Not repeatable JSON destination path on the node. It must be writable by the Riak service account. The short spelling is `-o`.

title: Combine queries and accumulate results

title: Combine queries and accumulate results
heading: Combine them#
text: Use `aggregation_expression` with references such as `$1` and `$2`. An example expression is `($1 INTERSECT $2) SUBTRACT $3`; the numbers must match the submitted tags. Use parentheses to make the intended grouping clear.

title: Combine queries and accumulate results
heading: Select accumulation#
text: Choose a mode supported for combination queries in the selected release. Use keys to inspect membership before switching to a count. Raw match counts and distinct-object counts are different when more than one index entry matches a key.

title: Combine queries and accumulate results
heading: Verify and retain the query#
text: Compare the combined result with the expected intersection, union, or subtraction of your independent query results. Include duplicate terms and an empty constituent result. Save the query body and expected answer as an application fixture so changes to the term encoding do not silently change its meaning.

title: Retrieve paginated or asynchronous query results
text: Retrieve a larger query result using the delivery mechanism supported by the selected release. Keep the query definition and namespace stable between requests.

title: Retrieve paginated or asynchronous query results
heading: Continuation-based retrieval#
text: Submit a supported single query with an explicit `max_results` and compatible accumulation mode. Save the response body and inspect the `X-Riak-Continuation` header. If present, submit the same query with that opaque value as the JSON `continuation` field. Continue until the response has no continuation header. Treat HTTP and JSON errors separately from an empty successful result.

title: Retrieve paginated or asynchronous query results
heading: Continuation-based retrieval#
text: Do not create or decode a continuation token yourself. Check results against a known dataset, including multiple entries for the same key, before using the loop in an application.

title: Retrieve paginated or asynchronous query results
heading: Queued retrieval in 3.4.1#
text: For releases supporting `queue_raw_keys` and `queue_raw_terms`, save `result_queue` from the initial response and retrieve batches with GET on the same bucket’s query endpoint. URL-encode the queue reference and supply an explicit batch limit. Track query completion and remaining queued results.

title: Build and install from source
text: Build a release from its pinned source and dependencies when a suitable package is unavailable or you need a development build. Build in an isolated environment matching the intended deployment.

title: Build and install from source
heading: Choose the release and toolchain#
text: Check Platforms, architectures, and Erlang/OTP compatibility for the release’s OTP compatibility. Install the compiler, build tools, Git, and native development libraries required by the repository’s release-specific build instructions. Ensure that you use the same OTP major version for build and runtime unless the release explicitly supports another combination.

title: Build and install from source
heading: Choose the release and toolchain#
text: Install the compiler, build tools, Git, and native development libraries required by the repository’s release-specific build instructions. Ensure that you use the same OTP major version for build and runtime unless the release explicitly supports another combination. Clone the OpenRiak release repository and check out the exact release tag, verifying that it exists before building:

title: Build and install from source
heading: Choose the release and toolchain#
text: Ensure that you use the same OTP major version for build and runtime unless the release explicitly supports another combination. Clone the OpenRiak release repository and check out the exact release tag, verifying that it exists before building: Sh

title: Build and install from source
heading: Choose the release and toolchain#
text: Sh git clone https://github.com/OpenRiak/riak.git cd riak git tag --list

title: Build and install from source
heading: Choose the release and toolchain#
text: Select the tag for OpenRiak KV 3.4.0. Record the resulting commit with `git rev-parse HEAD`. Do not build a moving branch and label it as a released package.

title: Build and install from source
heading: Build and inspect#
text: Follow the checked-out repository’s `README` and `Makefile` for the release target and dependency installation. Preserve its pinned dependency revisions. Record compiler and OTP versions, the commit, and the build output alongside the resulting artifact.

title: Build and install from source
heading: Build and inspect#
text: Preserve its pinned dependency revisions. Record compiler and OTP versions, the commit, and the build output alongside the resulting artifact. Inspect the generated release’s `bin`, `etc`, and `lib` directories.

title: Build and install from source
heading: Build and inspect#
text: Record compiler and OTP versions, the commit, and the build output alongside the resulting artifact. Inspect the generated release’s `bin`, `etc`, and `lib` directories. Run the configuration check against a dedicated empty data directory, then start the release under a non-root service account with the required directory ownership.

title: Build and install from source
heading: Verify before deployment#
text: Complete Verify an installation and run the application’s integration tests on the built artifact. Package or archive the release with its configuration and provenance; do not copy a partially built source tree over a running node. Follow Upgrade an OpenRiak KV cluster for deployment into an existing cluster.

title: Run OpenRiak with persistent Docker storage
heading: Ubuntu 22.04
text: Set the host paths in `.env` to dedicated directories on the intended persistent filesystem. Check ownership, free space, and the service UID/GID settings before startup. Do not point two independent nodes at the same backend data directory.

title: Run OpenRiak with persistent Docker storage
heading: Start and verify persistence#
text: Run `docker compose config` and inspect the resolved mounts, image, names, and ports. Start with `docker compose up -d --no-build`, write a test object, and read it back. Stop the project with `docker compose down`, then start it again using the same files and directories.

title: Run OpenRiak with persistent Docker storage
heading: Start and verify persistence#
text: Start with `docker compose up -d --no-build`, write a test object, and read it back. Stop the project with `docker compose down`, then start it again using the same files and directories. Verify that the same object and node identity remain available.

title: Run OpenRiak with persistent Docker storage
heading: Replace or upgrade the container#
text: Keep the persistent paths stable and follow the cluster upgrade procedure. A new container image does not convert backend data or make arbitrary downgrade paths safe. Back up the required state using the backend’s procedure before a change that needs a recovery copy.

title: Configure and run a MapReduce job
text: Run an existing MapReduce job with explicit inputs and bounded output. MapReduce is deprecated; prefer direct keys, secondary indexes, or the Query API for new workloads where they meet the requirement.

title: Configure and run a MapReduce job
heading: Prepare a small job#
text: Use the request contract in MapReduce jobs and functions. Start with a short explicit list of bucket/key inputs instead of a full bucket scan. Verify every referenced Erlang or JavaScript function is available and permitted on all nodes that may execute it.

title: Configure and run a MapReduce job
heading: Submit and observe#
text: Send the job using the HTTP transport in HTTP MapReduce transport or the PB messages in MapReduce messages. Set an application timeout and keep only the phase outputs needed by the caller. Record request scope, result size, errors, and cluster load.

title: Configure and run a MapReduce job
heading: Verify semantics and capacity#
text: Compare results with a known fixture and test missing keys and function failures. Increase scope gradually while monitoring memory, queues, and latency. Do not assume a distributed job sees an atomic snapshot or that cancelling a client request instantly stops all work.

title: Configure and run a MapReduce job
heading: Verify semantics and capacity#
text: Increase scope gradually while monitoring memory, queues, and latency. Do not assume a distributed job sees an atomic snapshot or that cancelling a client request instantly stops all work. For an existing JavaScript-heavy workload, record runtime and sandbox requirements before an upgrade.

title: Configure and run a MapReduce job
heading: Verify semantics and capacity#
text: Do not assume a distributed job sees an atomic snapshot or that cancelling a client request instantly stops all work. For an existing JavaScript-heavy workload, record runtime and sandbox requirements before an upgrade. Evaluate a replacement query or application-side computation before investing in new MapReduce dependencies.

title: Configure legacy replication through NAT
text: Configure address translation for an existing legacy replication relationship when peers cannot reach the addresses advertised inside the source network.

title: Configure legacy replication through NAT
heading: Map every endpoint#
text: Record internal listener addresses, externally reachable addresses, translated ports, and the direction of each connection. Include cluster-manager discovery and data connections, not only the first bootstrap address. Confirm which legacy replication generation is in use.

title: Configure legacy replication through NAT
heading: Apply the generation-specific mapping#
text: Use the NAT-related settings and runtime controls in Legacy AAE and riak_repl settings and Legacy riak_repl runtime controls for that generation. Configure stable one-to-one mappings where required and apply them consistently to the nodes that advertise peer addresses. Do not reuse these legacy mappings as current-generation `replrtq_sinkpeers` configuration.

title: Configure legacy replication through NAT
heading: Verify discovery and reconnects#
text: Test from the actual remote network. Confirm initial connection, discovery of all required peers, and reconnection after one peer restarts. Write a sample and observe completed fullsync.

title: Configure legacy replication through NAT
heading: Verify discovery and reconnects#
text: Confirm initial connection, discovery of all required peers, and reconnection after one peer restarts. Write a sample and observe completed fullsync. If bootstrap succeeds but replication stalls, inspect the later advertised addresses and firewall rules before changing timeouts.

title: Develop an application using the Redis add-on
text: Design application behaviour around the verified Redis add-on contract, including stale values and failures. Complete the compatibility and read-through checks before making the add-on a production dependency.

title: Develop an application using the Redis add-on
heading: Define the mapping#
text: Document how application keys map to OpenRiak type, bucket, and key identifiers. Verify binary values, media types, and the largest expected payload. Do not assume Redis command names imply support for every Redis operation or atomicity guarantee.

title: Develop an application using the Redis add-on
heading: Preserve write semantics#
text: Use the add-on’s documented context and sibling handling, or keep writes on the direct OpenRiak API and treat the cache as a separate read path. Test concurrent updates and uncertain retries. Define how stale cached values are invalidated after writes and deletions.

title: Develop an application using the Redis add-on
heading: Test degraded operation#
text: Exercise cache eviction, timeout, upstream failure, and reconnects. Confirm that the application distinguishes a missing key from an unavailable service. Bound retry and fallback load so a cache outage cannot overwhelm the database.

title: Develop an application using the Redis add-on
heading: Test degraded operation#
text: Confirm that the application distinguishes a missing key from an unavailable service. Bound retry and fallback load so a cache outage cannot overwhelm the database. Keep direct API tests in the acceptance suite and record the exact supported add-on command subset with Redis add-on commands and configuration.

title: Evaluate experimental strong consistency
text: Evaluate the deprecated experimental strong-consistency interface only in an isolated cluster with a workload that explicitly requires its semantics. Ordinary object quorums do not enable this interface.

title: Evaluate experimental strong consistency
heading: Check the constraints#
text: Read Experimental strong-consistency interface for supported operations, feature limitations, and bucket-type requirements. You should check for incompatible indexes, data types, replication, and client features before creating test data.

title: Evaluate experimental strong consistency
heading: Prepare a dedicated type#
text: Enable the required experimental configuration from Experimental strong-consistency interface, validate it, and create a dedicated type using Create and activate bucket types with the documented consistency property and replica policy. Do not change a populated ordinary type in place and assume its data has become an ensemble-managed dataset.

title: Evaluate experimental strong consistency
heading: Exercise the failure model#

title: Implement a legacy replication hook
text: Implement a callback that filters or supplements objects on an existing legacy `riak_repl` path. These hooks do not configure current-generation replication.

title: Implement a legacy replication hook
heading: Implement the contract#
text: Use the callback signatures and return values in Replication hook interface. Keep the callbacks bounded and avoid recursive writes or blocking external dependencies. Test `ok`, `cancel`, and any additional-object return path separately; filtering can intentionally leave clusters with different data.

title: Implement a legacy replication hook
heading: Register and distribute#
text: Compile the module for the target OTP and deploy it to every node that may execute the hook. Register it as a `repl_helper` through the extension registration interface in Custom code and hook interfaces, and verify that the expected module is loaded before enabling the relationship.

title: Implement a legacy replication hook
heading: Test real-time and fullsync paths#
text: Send allowed and blocked sample objects and verify both real-time delivery and a later fullsync. For an additional-object list, confirm the dependency objects arrive before the original object. Test callback errors in an isolated cluster and verify monitoring makes failures visible.

title: Implement a legacy replication hook
heading: Test real-time and fullsync paths#
text: For an additional-object list, confirm the dependency objects arrive before the original object. Test callback errors in an isolated cluster and verify monitoring makes failures visible. Remove the hook registration before removing its code during rollback.

title: Implement a legacy replication hook
heading: Test real-time and fullsync paths#
text: Test callback errors in an isolated cluster and verify monitoring makes failures visible. Remove the hook registration before removing its code during rollback. Reconcile or explicitly account for objects previously filtered out.

title: Maintain a legacy LevelDB deployment
text: Maintain an existing deployment using LevelDB while planning its migration. These interfaces have compatibility and deprecation constraints; check Feature status and deprecations before choosing them for new data.

title: Maintain a legacy LevelDB deployment
heading: Inventory the current state#
text: Record the exact release, backend configuration, affected buckets, stored-data size, and recovery method. Read the settings in Legacy LevelDB settings and compare them with the node’s effective configuration rather than assuming old defaults still apply.

title: Maintain a legacy LevelDB deployment
heading: Make a controlled change#
text: Check compaction pressure, cache memory, open files, and free space over a complete workload cycle. Keep the existing on-disk format and compression choices compatible with any planned recovery release. Back up the relevant state and test the change on representative data.

title: Maintain a legacy LevelDB deployment

title: Maintain a legacy LevelDB deployment
heading: Verify and plan migration#
text: Check known values, indexes where supported, memory and disk behaviour, and recovery after a stopped member. Use Migrate to another storage backend to migrate to another backend through a prepared destination, then retire the old state only after application verification.

text: Account for loss of local data whenever a process stops. A normal rolling restart does not transfer the old in-memory contents first; retain adequate replicas and a tested repair or reload path. Back up the relevant state and test the change on representative data.

title: Maintain legacy active anti-entropy
heading: Inspect the existing configuration#
text: Record tree storage, build schedules, exchange concurrency, and resource use. Legacy AAE uses separate stores and is distinct from TicTac AAE; changing one subsystem’s setting does not tune the other.

title: Maintain legacy active anti-entropy
heading: Apply and verify a change#
text: Validate the configuration and deploy it to a pilot node. Observe tree builds and exchanges over a full scheduled cycle, checking client latency and disk capacity. Keep rebuild and exchange pressure bounded rather than increasing concurrency after every timeout.

title: Maintain legacy active anti-entropy
heading: Transition protection#
text: Enable TicTac using Enable TicTac anti-entropy and wait for its initial stores and trees before disabling the old mechanism. The mechanisms can overlap during a transition. Verify current repair and reconciliation requirements, then remove obsolete legacy files only after the deployment no longer uses them and the recovery plan permits it.

title: Maintain legacy v2 replication
text: Assess and maintain a deployment that still uses legacy v2 replication. Do not mix v2 peer and fullsync commands with current-generation replication queues.

title: Maintain legacy v2 replication
heading: Identify the actual protocol#
text: Record both clusters’ versions, listener/client configuration, TLS settings, and bucket replication policy. Check Replication-generation compatibility and the availability labels in Legacy riak_repl runtime controls before issuing a command; an old runbook may name a command that is not supported by the selected release.

title: Maintain legacy v2 replication
heading: Verify the existing relationship#
text: Inspect source and destination status through the available legacy controls. Write, update, and delete a unique test key and confirm delivery. Check fullsync completion as well as real-time status.

title: Maintain legacy v2 replication
heading: Verify the existing relationship#
text: Write, update, and delete a unique test key and confirm delivery. Check fullsync completion as well as real-time status. Preserve the working configuration before changing peers or certificates.

title: Maintain legacy v2 replication
heading: Plan a supported transition#
text: Prefer moving to current-generation replication using Connect clusters with next-generation replication. Establish its source queues and consumers independently, seed and reconcile, and verify the application before retiring the old relationship. Keep rollback and conflict handling explicit if both paths are temporarily active.

title: Maintain legacy v2 replication
heading: Plan a supported transition#
text: Establish its source queues and consumers independently, seed and reconcile, and verify the application before retiring the old relationship. Keep rollback and conflict handling explicit if both paths are temporarily active. Do not infer protocol compatibility from a shared `riak repl` executable name.

Preserve the existing settings and avoid mixing v2 listener configuration with v3 cluster-manager configuration. For certificate changes use Secure legacy replication connections, and for translated addresses use Configure legacy replication through NAT.

title: Maintain legacy v3 replication

text: Write, update, and delete a sample through the normal application path. Confirm arrival and completed legacy fullsync; a connected status alone is insufficient. Monitor the workload during fullsync and investigate repeated rebuild or exchange failures.

title: Maintain legacy v3 replication

For a new relationship or a migration away from deprecated replication, follow Connect clusters with next-generation replication and verify the new path before retiring this one.

title: Maintain multi-backend and prefix routing
text: Maintain an existing deployment using multi-backend and prefix routing while planning its migration. These interfaces have compatibility and deprecation constraints; check Feature status and deprecations before choosing them for new data.

title: Maintain multi-backend and prefix routing
heading: Inventory the current state#
text: Record the exact release, backend configuration, affected buckets, stored-data size, and recovery method. Read the settings in Multi-backend and prefix-routing settings and compare them with the node’s effective configuration rather than assuming old defaults still apply.

title: Maintain multi-backend and prefix routing
heading: Make a controlled change#
text: Inventory every backend name and bucket-to-backend mapping before changing routing. A mapping change does not move existing data. Verify both typed and untyped buckets and preserve the old stores until migration is complete.

title: Maintain multi-backend and prefix routing
heading: Make a controlled change#
text: A mapping change does not move existing data. Verify both typed and untyped buckets and preserve the old stores until migration is complete. Back up the relevant state and test the change on representative data.

title: Maintain multi-backend and prefix routing
heading: Make a controlled change#
text: Verify both typed and untyped buckets and preserve the old stores until migration is complete. Back up the relevant state and test the change on representative data. Validate configuration before a rolling deployment and preserve a rollback path that does not mix incompatible store formats.

title: Maintain multi-backend and prefix routing
heading: Verify and plan migration#
text: Check known values, indexes where supported, memory and disk behaviour, and recovery after a stopped member. Use Migrate to another storage backend to migrate to another backend through a prepared destination, then retire the old state only after application verification.

title: Secure legacy replication connections
text: Protect an existing legacy replication relationship using its generation-specific TLS configuration. Keep the previous working files and a recovery path during certificate changes.

title: Secure legacy replication connections
heading: Prepare identities and trust#
text: Record the identities and trust roots expected at both ends. Check certificate names, validity, matching private keys, and readable PEM paths. Do not assume the current-generation `repl_*` certificate settings configure `riak_repl`.

title: Secure legacy replication connections
heading: Configure the legacy transport#
text: Use Legacy AAE and riak_repl settings for the available legacy TLS settings and Legacy riak_repl runtime controls for any required runtime controls. Apply the peer-name and trust policy consistently, then reload or restart according to the supported mechanism for the installed release.

title: Secure legacy replication connections
heading: Verify both authentication and delivery#
text: Confirm a connection with the trusted peer, rejection of an untrusted certificate, and delivery of a new sample object. Recheck fullsync after the transport change. Monitor expiry independently; do not assume Riak will renew certificates automatically.

title: Secure legacy replication connections
heading: Verify both authentication and delivery#
text: Recheck fullsync after the transport change. Monitor expiry independently; do not assume Riak will renew certificates automatically. During rotation, deploy new trust before changing peer certificates and remove old trust only after all peers have moved and the rollback interval has ended.

title: Set up a compatible Redis add-on deployment
text: Prepare an isolated compatibility test before deploying the historical Redis add-on with this OpenRiak release. A verified add-on package and compatibility matrix are not included in the current release metadata.

title: Set up a compatible Redis add-on deployment
heading: Establish a reproducible candidate#
text: Record the add-on source revision or package, Redis version, OTP version, and OpenRiak package. Check that the candidate supports the intended bucket-type and security interfaces. Do not install an old binary or obsolete distribution repository merely because a historical guide used it.

title: Set up a compatible Redis add-on deployment
heading: Isolate the test#
text: Keep Redis, the add-on, and OpenRiak on a private test network with disposable data. Configure authentication, resource limits, cache bounds, and the add-on’s connection settings using that candidate’s own version-matched instructions. Use Verify an installation to verify OpenRiak independently before introducing the proxy.

title: Set up a compatible Redis add-on deployment
heading: Accept or reject compatibility#
text: Run the read-through, write, delete, expiry, sibling, and outage checks in Use and monitor the Redis add-on and Develop an application using the Redis add-on. Record the exact versions and results. Until these checks pass, use the normal OpenRiak client interface for the deployment.

title: Use and monitor the Redis add-on
text: Verify read-through and failure behaviour in an isolated Redis add-on deployment whose exact versions have been recorded with Set up a compatible Redis add-on deployment.

title: Use and monitor the Redis add-on
heading: Check the source of truth#
text: Write a unique known object directly to OpenRiak, read it directly, then request it through the add-on’s documented key mapping. Compare the bytes and content interpretation. Repeat after warming the cache.

title: Use and monitor the Redis add-on
heading: Exercise changes and failures#
text: Update the value with causal context, delete it, and allow cache entries to expire. Observe when each change becomes visible through the add-on. Stop Redis, then the add-on, then one OpenRiak test member in separate runs; verify whether requests fail, fall back, or return stale data according to the candidate’s contract.

title: Use and monitor the Redis add-on
heading: Monitor the full path#
text: Measure cache hits and misses, evictions, memory, upstream errors, and request latency at both layers. Compare cached results with direct reads of known keys. A healthy Redis process alone does not establish that the backing data path works.

title: Use and monitor the Redis add-on
heading: Monitor the full path#

title: Use and monitor the Redis add-on

text: A healthy Redis process alone does not establish that the backing data path works. Retain the compatibility record and reset the disposable data when finished. Do not generalize the result to untested add-on or Redis versions.

text: Compare request-rate and latency metrics with CPU, memory, disk I/O, open files, and logs for the same interval. Use Node and cluster metrics for metric definitions. Take repeated samples; cumulative counters need a time delta and may reset when a node restarts.

title: Inspect node and cluster health
heading: Narrow the investigation#
text: Use vnode status for a local partition problem, worker-queue inspection for delayed background work, and the remote console only when ordinary metrics are insufficient. Preserve the initial evidence before restarting a failing node. Verify improvement through the original client request, not only through a changed status line.

text: Inspect a small set of known objects and their metadata when diagnosing a data problem. Start with the public API so you can compare what the application sees.

heading: Compare and retain context#
text: Compare the internal object with the API representation and the application’s expected encoding. Use bounded AAE statistics or key-finding folds for a wider pattern. Do not rewrite the inspected object unless you have a defined repair or conflict-resolution rule.

title: Inspect vnode and backend status
heading: Correlate the evidence#
text: Check whether the partition is primary, fallback, or transferring ownership. Compare its backend errors, file or store state, queues, and recent log events with client failures at the same time. A busy vnode during handoff is a different diagnosis from a store that cannot open its files.

title: Inspect vnode and backend status
heading: Choose the next action#
text: Preserve logs and status before restarting or repairing. Use the backend-specific repair procedure only after identifying the scope. After a corrective action, repeat the same status capture and verify representative object reads and indexed queries.

title: Inspect worker queues and saturation
text: Identify worker queues that delay background operations and distinguish insufficient processing capacity from excessive submitted work.

title: Inspect worker queues and saturation
heading: Collect a time series#
text: Record queue lengths, active workers, completed operations, timeout logs, backend latency, and client request percentiles over the same interval. Use AAE, repair, and worker-pool metrics for the release’s metrics and Repair and handoff settings for worker-related settings.

title: Inspect worker queues and saturation
heading: Find the producer#
text: Correlate growth with AAE rebuilds, fullsync checks, folds, handoffs, or bulk reclamation jobs. A job timing out while queued can waste backend work even after the caller has stopped waiting. Reduce overlapping schedules or narrow the submitted scope before increasing concurrency.

title: Inspect worker queues and saturation
heading: Adjust one limit at a time#
text: Change the appropriate pool or request budget on a pilot node. More workers can saturate storage and increase application latency; retain a measured recovery-progress target as well as a client latency target.

title: Inspect worker queues and saturation
heading: Verify and persist#
text: Confirm that the queue drains, useful operations complete, and request latency remains acceptable. Persist any lasting configuration change and restore temporary diagnostic overrides. If work still accumulates, address the underlying I/O or workload limit rather than repeatedly extending timeouts.

title: Investigate read-repair activity
text: Investigate increased read-repair work by correlating it with recent failures, ownership changes, and application traffic.

title: Investigate read-repair activity
heading: Establish the pattern#
text: Measure read-repair activity as a rate over time and compare nodes. Record concurrent client errors, request latency, handoffs, restarts, and AAE discrepancies. A repair after a temporary outage can be expected; a sustained increase without recovery needs explanation.

title: Investigate read-repair activity
heading: Inspect representative keys#
text: Choose a small sample associated with the problem and compare values, siblings, and causal context through the normal API. Check that clients preserve context and that bucket replica policies are consistent. Avoid exhaustive key listing as the first diagnostic step.

title: Investigate read-repair activity
heading: Resolve the cause#
text: Allow expected handoffs to complete, repair lost data through Repair a vnode or node from surviving replicas, or correct application conflict handling through Resolve concurrent object updates. If cold data remains divergent, verify TicTac AAE rather than relying on future reads to discover it.

title: Investigate read-repair activity
heading: Verify#
text: Compare repair rates and client latency after the fix. A lower counter alone is not enough: confirm the affected keys are present and the required background protection is still running.

title: Monitor anti-entropy progress

title: Monitor anti-entropy progress

text: Correlate AAE logs with metrics from AAE, repair, and worker-pool metrics. Track completed work and changing discrepancy counts over time. A recurring timeout or a queue that only grows means you should review worker capacity and backend I/O before increasing exchange frequency.

text: Use Rebuild AAE trees when a tree rebuild is required, Repair a selected key range for a bounded key repair, and Repair a vnode or node from surviving replicas for lost vnode data. Keep token-bucket protection enabled while diagnosing pressure. After intervention, repeat the same observations and verify representative object reads.

title: Monitor replication and inter-cluster reconciliation

text: Verify queue names, filters, destination type definitions, peer reachability, and recent source restarts. Temporary queues can lose references; use reconciliation or a bounded re-seed to recover them. Do not clear a queue as a routine lag remedy.

title: Configure a load-balancing proxy
text: Put a proxy in front of client listeners when applications need a stable endpoint or coordinated connection draining. Keep Erlang distribution and administrative commands on their own network path.

title: Configure a load-balancing proxy
heading: Choose the proxy mode#
text: Use HTTP-aware proxying for the HTTP API, or TCP proxying for Protocol Buffers. Configure TLS termination or passthrough according to where authentication and certificate validation occur. Forward authorization, causal-context, conditional-request, and content-type headers unchanged.

title: Configure a load-balancing proxy

Use `/ping` for a basic HTTP liveness check, and supplement it with cluster monitoring; liveness does not prove healthy replicas or an acceptable workload. Choose connection and response timeouts long enough for the application’s supported operations, with explicit limits for long-running queries.

title: Configure a load-balancing proxy
heading: Verify the real client path#
text: Through the proxy, test an authenticated read, a write with causal context, a conditional failure, a missing key, and the largest expected response. Test PB connections separately if used. Confirm that a failed upstream is removed and that healthy members still serve requests.

title: Configure a load-balancing proxy
heading: Drain for maintenance#
text: Remove one node from the proxy’s active upstreams, allow existing connections to finish, and perform the node maintenance. Return it only after process, membership, and application checks pass. Keep enough healthy upstream capacity for the remaining workload.

title: Configure object expiration
heading: Apply a small test#
text: Set the backend-specific expiry enablement and retention interval on every affected node. Validate, restart as required, and write uniquely named sample objects before and after the change. Do not assume previously stored objects acquire an expiry schedule retroactively.

title: Configure object expiration
heading: Verify retention and reclamation#
text: Read samples before and after the interval, update one sample partway through, and repeat the test after a node outage and replication catch-up. Check both read behaviour and eventual disk reclamation; a logically expired value and a removed file are different states. If the behaviour does not meet the policy, disable new expiry according to the schema and investigate before applying it more broadly.

title: Set runtime environment variables
text: Change an Erlang application environment value on a running node when the target component supports reading it at runtime. A successful environment update does not mean a process that cached the value has reconfigured itself.

title: Set runtime environment variables
heading: Identify the exact key#
text: Use All configuration settings and defaults to find the application name, internal setting name, and data type. Check the component’s runtime control interface first; a dedicated function may update active processes as well as the environment.

title: Set runtime environment variables
heading: Record and change#
text: Open the remote console using Inspect a node through the remote console. Read the existing value with Erlang’s `application:get_env/2`, record it, then use `application:set_env/3` with the exact application, key, and Erlang value. Apply the change only to the intended nodes; this API changes the local VM unless a separate cluster-wide function is documented.

title: Set runtime environment variables
heading: Verify and persist#
text: Read the environment back and exercise the affected feature. Compare logs, metrics, and request behaviour. If the component requires a restart or a dedicated refresh, schedule that explicitly.

title: Set runtime environment variables

title: Benchmark a representative workload
text: Benchmark the intended workload and failure states before choosing capacity or tuning values. A short run against empty storage is not a reliable capacity measurement.

title: Benchmark a representative workload
heading: Define the workload#
text: Record key count, object-size distribution, read/write/delete mix, concurrency, conflict rate, index/query patterns, and client retry policy. Include authentication, TLS, and the actual network path. Use a fixed seed or recorded dataset when repeatability matters.

title: Benchmark a representative workload
heading: Prepare a representative environment#
text: Use the target package, OTP, backend, filesystem, and replica policies. Load enough data to exercise normal memory and disk behaviour, then allow maintenance to reach a steady cycle. Keep the load generator separate and verify it is not the bottleneck.

title: Benchmark a representative workload
heading: Run and measure#
text: Increase load in controlled steps while recording achieved throughput, latency percentiles, errors, CPU, memory, disk I/O, queues, and maintenance logs. Include a stable sustained period and a recovery period. Test a rolling restart or failed member at the intended operating load, using only disposable or approved test data.

title: Benchmark a representative workload
heading: Compare changes#
text: Change one relevant variable, rerun the same workload, and compare both client and recovery outcomes. Preserve tool version, dataset, commands, configuration, and raw results. Adopt a change only if it improves the target metric without violating the other operating limits.

title: Reduce Query API cost
text: Reduce Query API cost by changing a measured part of the query while preserving its answer.

title: Reduce Query API cost
heading: Record a baseline#
text: Save the request body, result, latency distribution, dataset size, and concurrent workload. Measure several executions, including a normal background-work period. Record the index range scanned and result size separately.

title: Reduce Query API cost
heading: Make one change#
text: Narrow the ordered range when the current scan examines many irrelevant terms. Project attributes needed for filtering to avoid fetching every candidate object. Simplify an expensive evaluation or filter expression without changing its predicate. Return counts or grouped counts when the caller does not need every key. Use the supported bounded delivery mode when response size dominates memory or transport.

title: Reduce Query API cost
heading: Verify correctness and impact#
text: You should verify your results by comparing against the same known dataset, including boundary and duplicate cases. Measure tail latency, worker queues, backend load, and the effect on writes and repair. Retain a change only when it improves the intended metric without violating the application’s result contract.

title: Reduce Query API cost
heading: Verify correctness and impact#
text: Measure tail latency, worker queues, backend load, and the effect on writes and repair. Retain a change only when it improves the intended metric without violating the application’s result contract. If extra concurrency merely lengthens queues, reduce offered work or address the constrained resource rather than raising timeouts.

title: Reduce request latency
text: Reduce request latency by identifying where time is spent before changing database limits. Compare the same workload and percentile before and after each change.

title: Reduce request latency
heading: Localise the delay#
text: Separate client/proxy time, network time, coordinator queues, replica response time, and backend I/O. Compare affected nodes and operations. Large values, many siblings, storage maintenance, and overloaded worker queues require different fixes.

title: Reduce request latency
heading: Choose the smallest useful change#
text: Reduce oversized object boundaries or resolve sibling growth in the application. Stagger Bitcask maintenance when it is the measured cause. For saturated storage, reduce overlapping background work or add capacity.

title: Reduce request latency
heading: Choose the smallest useful change#
text: Stagger Bitcask maintenance when it is the measured cause. For saturated storage, reduce overlapping background work or add capacity. Change acknowledgement policies only when the application’s durability and availability requirements permit it.

title: Reduce request latency
heading: Verify under load#
text: Run the representative benchmark through the real client path, including a maintenance or recovery interval. Confirm improved tail latency without increased errors, lost protection, or an ever-growing background backlog. Keep the original configuration and revert changes that merely move the bottleneck elsewhere.

title: Set and verify file-descriptor limits
text: Set the open-file limit for the actual Riak service process, then verify that it inherited the intended value. A shell’s `ulimit` does not necessarily control a service manager’s child process.

title: Set and verify file-descriptor limits
heading: Measure usage and limits#
text: Identify the Riak BEAM process from the service or container, then inspect `/proc/PID/limits` and `/proc/PID/fd` on Linux. Compare current descriptor use with the backend’s files, client connections, and expected recovery workload.

title: Set and verify file-descriptor limits
heading: Configure the owning launcher#
text: For systemd, set `LimitNOFILE` in a service override and reload the manager before a controlled restart. For OpenRC or a direct launcher, use the service’s supported limits configuration. For Docker, set the service’s `ulimits.nofile` in Compose.

title: Set and verify file-descriptor limits
heading: Configure the owning launcher#
text: For OpenRC or a direct launcher, use the service’s supported limits configuration. For Docker, set the service’s `ulimits.nofile` in Compose. Choose a limit based on the workload and host capacity rather than copying an unrelated shell example.

title: Set and verify file-descriptor limits
heading: Verify after restart#
text: Read the running process’s limits again and check logs for open-file errors. Exercise expected peak connections and storage activity. Monitor descriptor growth over time; raising the limit does not fix a leak or an unbounded client connection pool.

title: Tune a deployment on AWS
text: Tune an AWS deployment from measured instance, storage, and network behaviour. Keep a stable production workload and recovery target when comparing infrastructure choices.

title: Tune a deployment on AWS
heading: Identify the limiting resource#
text: Compare Riak latency and match growth with EC2 CPU, network, and EBS latency/throughput observations. Check whether the instance or volume is reaching its provisioned or burst limits. Include cross-zone traffic and recovery transfers in the measurement.

title: Tune a deployment on AWS
heading: Test a specific change#
text: Benchmark the same dataset on candidate instance and volume configurations. Evaluate sustained behaviour after burst capacity is exhausted. Preserve node identity and data during infrastructure changes, and use a planned replacement when moving storage or instance families.

title: Tune a deployment on AWS
heading: Verify resilience and cost#
text: Rehearse one unavailable member and a rolling replacement. Confirm that the surviving deployment meets application latency and recovery targets. Review retained EBS backups, transfer charges, and unused resources along with compute cost; compare measured total capacity rather than a nominal instance specification.

title: Tune a deployment on AWS
heading: Verify resilience and cost#
text: Confirm that the surviving deployment meets application latency and recovery targets. Review retained EBS backups, transfer charges, and unused resources along with compute cost; compare measured total capacity rather than a nominal instance specification. Use current AWS instance and EBS documentation for the selected Region’s supported combinations and limits.

title: Tune a deployment on AWS
heading: Verify resilience and cost#
text: Review retained EBS backups, transfer charges, and unused resources along with compute cost; compare measured total capacity rather than a nominal instance specification. Use current AWS instance and EBS documentation for the selected Region’s supported combinations and limits. For a disposable first deployment, follow Build a learning cluster on AWS EC2.

title: Tune filesystems, memory, and network settings
text: Tune host storage, memory, and networking only when measurements show they constrain the workload. Record the host and kernel versions alongside any persistent change.

title: Tune filesystems, memory, and network settings
heading: Inspect the actual environment#
text: Check filesystem type and mount options, device latency and queueing, free space, memory pressure and swap activity, network errors, and the process’s resource limits. Include container constraints and cloud volume limits where applicable.

title: Tune filesystems, memory, and network settings
heading: Change one layer at a time#
text: Prefer fixing insufficient I/O capacity or an unsuitable storage layout over masking it with longer timeouts. Test filesystem and I/O scheduler choices on the actual device. Evaluate memory and huge-page policies with the intended OTP and backend rather than applying a universal sysctl list.

title: Tune filesystems, memory, and network settings
heading: Verify persistence and behaviour#
text: Apply a candidate change to a test/pilot node, repeat the workload through a maintenance cycle, and verify the setting survives reboot if that is intended. Compare request percentiles, errors, background completion, and memory headroom. Revert changes that improve a microbenchmark but worsen the database workload.

title: Tune replication throughput and lag
text: Adjust replication throughput while keeping both clusters’ application workloads within their latency targets.

title: Tune replication throughput and lag
heading: Measure the bottleneck#
text: Record source queue growth and discards, sink fetch/push timings, delivery lag, network latency, and destination backend pressure. Separate slow real-time delivery from slow fullsync discovery.

title: Tune replication throughput and lag
heading: Adjust consumers carefully#
text: Use the sink-worker and per-peer limits in Next-generation replication settings or the runtime controls in Next-generation replication runtime controls. Increase in small steps only while both sides have spare capacity. More consumers can overload a concentrated backlog of keys on a few vnodes.

title: Tune replication throughput and lag
heading: Balance reconciliation#
text: Reduce overlapping checks that time out before completing. For a large known gap, use a bounded seed rather than increasing every fullsync limit. Consider compression only when data is compressible and CPU headroom exists.

title: Tune replication throughput and lag
heading: Verify the full cycle#
text: Pause and resume a consumer in a test environment, measure catch-up, and confirm a completed in-sync exchange. Persist successful settings and restore temporary runtime changes. Do not accept a lower lag measurement if discard counters increase or application latency degrades.

title: Tune the Erlang VM for a measured bottleneck
text: Tune the Erlang VM only for a measured bottleneck and with a repeatable rollback. Keep the package’s baseline values until evidence identifies a limit worth changing.

title: Tune the Erlang VM for a measured bottleneck
heading: Capture the baseline#
text: Record the OTP version, scheduler and process activity, memory categories, port usage, distribution pressure, and client latency. Use Investigate a running node with Erlang diagnostics for bounded runtime diagnostics and Erlang VM and runtime settings for the release’s VM settings.

title: Tune the Erlang VM for a measured bottleneck
heading: Select one hypothesis#
text: For example, distinguish scheduler saturation from waiting on storage before changing scheduler counts. Check actual process or port usage before increasing limits. Consider container CPU and memory constraints; the VM cannot make unavailable host resources appear.

title: Tune the Erlang VM for a measured bottleneck
heading: Apply to a pilot#
text: Change the persistent VM setting through the supported configuration path, validate, and restart a pilot member. Keep the old configuration and the exact baseline workload. Avoid changing several interacting scheduler, GC, and buffer options at once.

title: Tune the Erlang VM for a measured bottleneck
heading: Compare and roll out#
text: Measure both throughput and tail latency, memory headroom, and recovery behaviour. Revert if the target improves at an unacceptable cost elsewhere. Apply a successful change through a rolling restart and verify the effective VM arguments on every member.

title: Check production readiness
text: Check a deployment before sending production traffic. Keep the evidence with the release and infrastructure configuration so the checks can be repeated after changes.

title: Check production readiness
heading: Confirm the deployment#
text: Verify package versions, OTP variants, architecture, and backend on every member. Confirm unique stable node identities, compatible ring settings, and the intended membership and ownership plan. Check that data directories survive process and host restarts and have sufficient capacity for recovery. Restrict client, distribution, and administrative access to the intended networks and identities.

title: Check production readiness
heading: Exercise the application#
text: Run representative create, read, update, delete, index, and conflict-resolution operations to verify timeout and retry behaviour, missing-object handling, and causal-context preservation. Test with the actual authentication and TLS configuration.

title: Check production readiness
heading: Prove operational recovery#
text: Rehearse a rolling restart, a failed-node recovery, and a restore in an isolated environment. If replication is used, pause and resume a consumer and prove reconciliation. Confirm that monitoring detects unavailable nodes, growing queues, disk pressure, and elevated request latency.

title: Check production readiness
heading: Record the operating limits#
text: Document measured capacity, expansion triggers, backup retention, recovery targets, and who can execute administrative changes. Resolve failed checks before enabling traffic; repeat the relevant checks when the package, workload, or infrastructure changes.

title: Choose a deletion and retention policy
text: Choose how long deleted or expired data remains recoverable and how storage is reclaimed. Apply the policy consistently across replicating clusters.

title: Choose a deletion and retention policy
heading: Select deletion behaviour#
text: For replicated deployments, retain tombstones long enough for every destination and temporarily unavailable replica to observe deletion. Review the current values rather than assuming a package default:

title: Choose a deletion and retention policy
heading: Select deletion behaviour#
text: Review the current values rather than assuming a package default: Config name `delete_mode` Application name `riak_kv.delete_mode` Description Feature: deletionSource repository: riak_kvSource module: riak_kv_eraserSource module: riak_kv_vnodeConcept: retentionConcept: tombstonesChoose how long delete tombstones remain: `keep` retains them for explicit reaping, `immediate` removes them immediately, and an integer number of milliseconds delays removal. Retaining tombstones allows deletes to reach replicas and connected clusters; early removal can allow older copies to reappear. Use a consistent policy across reconciling clusters.

title: Choose a deletion and retention policy
heading: Select deletion behaviour#
text: NotesChecked against the delete-mode schema validator. Its error message says “between 0 and 300000”, but the implementation uses `Value > 0` and `Value < 300000`. The same checks apply in 3.4.0 and 3.4.1.

title: Choose a deletion and retention policy
heading: Select deletion behaviour#
text: Reference sources Annotations: delete_mode/common.md. delete_mode Set the delete_mode for the node (should be set to the same value across all reconciling clusters). There are three options: - keep (recommended) - immediate - Milliseconds (default = 3000) If delete_mode is set to keep, every delete will leave a permanent tombstone, that will need to be reaped at a later date (i.e. once tombstones have been securely replicated around connected clusters). This will minimise the chance that values are resurrected through anti-entropy processes.

title: Choose a deletion and retention policy
heading: Select deletion behaviour#

This will minimise the chance that values are resurrected through anti-entropy processes. If delete_mode is immediate, then tombstones are not used - every delete is a direct delete in the backend (though that may involve a backend tombstone).

title: Choose a deletion and retention policy
heading: Select deletion behaviour#
text: Use `keep` when tombstones will be reaped explicitly after reconciliation. Account for that retained storage in capacity planning. A time-based delete mode needs an outage and reconciliation policy compatible with its retention period.

title: Choose a deletion and retention policy
heading: Decide whether expiration is suitable#
text: Use object expiration only when the application’s retention rule matches backend support and the timestamp semantics. Test reads, updates, replication, and reappearance after an outage before enabling it for existing data. Expiration is not a substitute for an application audit or an immutable history.

title: Choose a deletion and retention policy
heading: Schedule reclamation#
text: First count or list the intended scope. Complete required reconciliation before erasing objects or reaping tombstones, and avoid overlapping reaping with membership changes. Start with a small range and monitor client latency and worker queues.

title: Choose a deletion and retention policy
heading: Verify#
text: To verify the policy, you should read known live and deleted samples from all receiving clusters. Check that expired data is handled as expected and that maintenance eventually releases space without resurrecting deleted values.

title: Choose a multi-cluster topology
text: Choose the direction and purpose of every inter-cluster replication relationship. Separate application availability, disaster recovery, migration, and backup requirements before configuring peers.

title: Choose a multi-cluster topology
heading: Draw the data paths#
text: For each cluster, list the applications allowed to write, which buckets must be received, the permitted recovery lag, and the intended failover procedure. Use one-way replication for a destination that should not originate application updates. Use bidirectional paths when both sides write and the application can resolve conflicts.

title: Choose a multi-cluster topology
heading: Define direct relationships#
text: Create a separate source queue for each independent destination. A replicated push does not automatically become a new real-time event for a third cluster, so do not assume a chain will relay updates. Configure the required direct peer relationships and matching bucket types.

title: Choose a multi-cluster topology
heading: Plan reconciliation and cutover#
text: Pair real-time delivery with reconciliation. Reserve capacity for a backlog after an outage and test the failover endpoint switch. Define how credentials, bucket properties, certificates, and other cluster metadata are provisioned separately; object replication does not copy those items.

title: Choose a multi-cluster topology
heading: Verify the topology#
text: You should write a distinct sample in each permitted source and confirm its appearance only at intended destinations. Pause a consumer, create changes, and prove catch-up and reconciliation before relying on the topology.

title: Choose a ring size
text: Choose the partition count before a new cluster receives data. The ring controls how work is divided into virtual nodes; see Rings, partitions, and virtual nodes for the model.

title: Choose a ring size
heading: Estimate the deployment range#
text: Record the initial and expected maximum number of physical nodes, replication policy, and recovery-time target. Evaluate candidate power-of-two ring sizes in a test cluster with the intended backend. More partitions provide finer placement but also increase per-vnode overhead and maintenance work.

title: Choose a ring size
heading: Verify placement#
text: Join the test members, inspect the proposed ownership plan, and wait for handoffs to complete. Measure partition balance, vnode memory, startup time, and recovery under the expected largest deployment. Save the chosen value with the provisioning configuration.

title: Choose a storage backend
text: Select a backend according to required query features, data size, memory budget, and maintenance behaviour. Make the choice before loading a new node’s data.

title: Choose a storage backend
heading: Check required capabilities#
text: Use Backend capability matrix to check secondary indexes, Query API support, and backup capabilities. Choose Leveled when the application needs the current Query API. Evaluate Bitcask for direct-key workloads where its in-memory key directory fits the resource budget.

title: Choose a storage backend
heading: Check required capabilities#
text: Choose Leveled when the application needs the current Query API. Evaluate Bitcask for direct-key workloads where its in-memory key directory fits the resource budget. Treat deprecated backends as compatibility choices for existing deployments.

title: Choose a storage backend
heading: Measure with representative data#
text: Compare sustained write and read latency, startup time, disk use, maintenance I/O, and memory at the expected key count. Include deletion and compaction behaviour, not only a short empty-store benchmark.

heading: Configure and verify#

title: Choose a storage backend
heading: Configure and verify#
text: Write, update, delete, and query sample data through the required interfaces. Record the tested backend and filesystem in the deployment specification. For a populated deployment use Migrate to another storage backend; changing a setting alone does not migrate its files, it will simply be invisible to OpenRiak until the change is reverted.

title: Choose replication and acknowledgement policies
text: Choose replica and acknowledgement policies that meet the application’s failure and durability requirements. Use Quorums, availability, and durability and Causality, version vectors, and siblings if you need the relationship between replicas, causal context, and quorums.

title: Choose replication and acknowledgement policies
heading: State the failure requirement#
text: Record which node failures the application must tolerate, whether requests may use fallback replicas, and whether successful writes must be persisted to storage before acknowledgement. Quorum settings do not turn ordinary objects into linearizable transactions.

title: Choose replication and acknowledgement policies
heading: Define bucket-type policies#
text: Select `n_val` for replica count and the appropriate read/write acknowledgement properties for each data class. Check `r`, `pr`, `w`, `pw`, `dw`, `node_confirms`, and `sync_on_write` in Bucket properties and defaults. Use stricter request overrides only when the operation needs them, and handle timeout or insufficient-replica responses explicitly.

title: Choose replication and acknowledgement policies
heading: Test failure and ambiguity#
text: Create and activate a test bucket type, perform concurrent writes, then stop a test node and repeat the workload. Confirm both the accepted operations and rejected operations match the policy. A timed-out write may still have taken effect; retry with the application’s idempotency and causal-context rules.

title: Choose replication and acknowledgement policies
heading: Apply consistently#
text: Create matching type definitions in every receiving cluster before replicating typed objects. For a change to existing replica placement, rehearse migration or repair rather than assuming a property edit has already copied every object to the new replica set.

title: Map application data to objects and buckets
text: Design object keys, bucket boundaries, and query paths before committing to a storage layout. Start with the application’s reads and updates, including how it will resolve concurrent changes.

title: Map application data to objects and buckets
heading: List access patterns#
text: For each operation, record the identifier supplied by the caller, the fields returned, expected object size, read/write rate, and acceptable staleness. Prefer direct key lookups when the caller already has an identifier. For discovery by attributes, identify the required secondary indexes and confirm the backend capability in Backend capability matrix.

title: Map application data to objects and buckets
heading: Choose the object boundary#
text: Keep fields together when they are normally read and updated together. Separate independently updated or unbounded collections so one growing object does not become a contention or memory problem. Do not assume a transaction spans several keys.

title: Map application data to objects and buckets
heading: Choose the object boundary#
text: Separate independently updated or unbounded collections so one growing object does not become a contention or memory problem. Do not assume a transaction spans several keys. Choose stable keys that the application can reconstruct.

title: Map application data to objects and buckets
heading: Choose the object boundary#
text: Do not assume a transaction spans several keys. Choose stable keys that the application can reconstruct. Include a tenant or other namespace in the key or bucket when necessary, and apply one encoding consistently in every client.

title: Map application data to objects and buckets
heading: Choose the object boundary#
text: Choose stable keys that the application can reconstruct. Include a tenant or other namespace in the key or bucket when necessary, and apply one encoding consistently in every client. Store an explicit schema version if the value format will evolve.

title: Map application data to objects and buckets
heading: Assign policies#
text: Use bucket types to group data requiring the same conflict, durability, or data-type policy. Avoid creating a type per customer unless each truly needs a distinct policy. Define what a missing key means and how the application handles siblings, retries, and partial multi-object operations.

title: Map application data to objects and buckets
heading: Test the design#
text: Create representative objects, query them through each access path, then issue concurrent updates from two clients. Measure payload size and response latency with realistic distributions. Confirm that the application can merge conflicts and read both old and new schema versions before adopting the layout.

title: Size a cluster and reserve recovery headroom
text: Estimate capacity from a representative workload, then reserve room for failure recovery and maintenance. Use measurements from the intended backend and infrastructure.

title: Size a cluster and reserve recovery headroom
heading: Measure a baseline#
text: Record object count, stored bytes including indexes and metadata, working-set size, peak request rate, request mix, and latency percentiles. Measure disk space and I/O after compaction or merging reaches a steady cycle. Include replica storage and retained tombstones.

title: Size a cluster and reserve recovery headroom
heading: Model a failed member#
text: Calculate the per-node load with the intended number of surviving members. Reserve free space for ownership transfers, backend maintenance, and temporary replication queues. Check memory for Bitcask’s key directory or Leveled’s caches and concurrent requests; nominal disk capacity alone is insufficient.

title: Size a cluster and reserve recovery headroom
heading: Rehearse the limit#
text: Run a load test with production-like keys and values. Stop one test member, continue traffic, and measure recovery after it returns. Repeat the intended rolling maintenance operation.

title: Size a cluster and reserve recovery headroom
heading: Rehearse the limit#
text: Stop one test member, continue traffic, and measure recovery after it returns. Repeat the intended rolling maintenance operation. Choose a node count and resource size that meet the latency and recovery targets in those states, not only at idle.

title: Size a cluster and reserve recovery headroom
heading: Set expansion triggers#
text: You should set alerts for usable disk space, sustained device latency, queue growth, and request percentiles. Include provisioning and handoff time in the trigger threshold. Document the measured bottleneck, expected growth, and the next expansion step.

title: Start a local cluster with Docker
text: Start a local development cluster using the published cluster Compose file and verify that its nodes form one cluster.

heading: Ubuntu 22.04
text: Review `.env`, give the cluster a unique set of container names, and keep its config, data, logs, and shared control directory separate from other clusters. For local-only access, prefix each published host port with `127.0.0.1:`. The supplied services are `node1` through `node5`; exactly one is the coordinator.

title: Start a local cluster with Docker
heading: Stop and resume#
text: Run `docker compose down` in this directory to stop its services. Retain the bind mounts and control directory to resume the same cluster. For a fresh disposable cluster, remove only that project’s retained state after stopping it.

title: Start a local node with Docker
text: Start one local OpenRiak node with a published Docker Compose file, then verify an HTTP write and read. This is a disposable development environment.

title: Start a local node with Docker
heading: Before you begin#
text: Install Docker Engine or Docker Desktop with Compose, and have `curl` available. Create an empty working directory. Keep it separate from any existing cluster data.

title: Start a local node with Docker
heading: Download and start#
text: Select an operating system below. Download its Single Node Compose File and Example Environment File into the working directory. Save them as `compose.yaml` and `.env`.

title: Configure and schedule fullsync
text: Schedule TicTac fullsync checks and verify that discovered differences are delivered through the replication queues. Prepare source queues, sink workers, and usable AAE trees first.

heading: Configure one peer relationship per node#
text: Use different cluster slices for opposing clusters. Set an autocheck rate appropriate to the total number of participating nodes: a per-node schedule multiplies across the deployment. Prefer autochecks over overlapping fixed hour/day/range schedules unless you have a measured reason.

title: Configure and schedule fullsync
heading: Tune only from evidence#
text: Track exchange duration, timeouts, worker backlog, and repair counts. If jobs overlap or time out in queues, reduce scheduling pressure before increasing work limits. For a known large gap, seed the affected range using Re-replicate a key range or time window rather than repeatedly widening every fullsync request.

title: Configure replication queues and filters
text: Define source queues and filters so each destination receives the intended objects. Each independent destination needs its own queue on every source node.

title: Configure replication queues and filters
heading: Choose names and scope#
text: Use stable queue names describing their consumers. Select `any` for all eligible real-time changes, or the release’s bucket-type, bucket-name, or bucket-prefix filter for a subset. Name and prefix filters do not distinguish types by themselves; You should use a type filter when that distinction matters.

title: Configure replication queues and filters
heading: Choose names and scope#
text: Reference sources Annotations: replrtq_srcqueue/common.md. Queue definitions Queues should be defined using a pipe ‘|’ delimited string, of two colon ‘:’ delimited elements. The first part of each queue definition is the ascii name of the queue, the second part indicated the filter to be applied which should be either: - any (all real-time modifications to be replicated via this queue) - block_rtq (no real-time modifications to be replicated) - bucketname.<name_of_bucket> - bucketprefix.<prefix_for_bucket> - buckettype.<name_of_type> The latter three options allow for specific buckets to be supported by the queue, or only buckets with certain prefixes, or for just buckets of a given type.

heading: Apply and check capacity#
text: Apply the queue definitions consistently to every source node. Review memory and overflow limits in Next-generation replication settings, and monitor discard counters; persisted overflow is still a temporary queue, not a durable change log.

title: Configure replication queues and filters
heading: Verify inclusion and exclusion#
text: Write samples inside and outside each filter. Confirm intended consumers receive only their selected objects. Queue changes do not retroactively seed old objects, and dropping a queue discards pending work; plan reconciliation after changes.

text: Deliver a test write and deletion through the intended queue. Then test an untrusted certificate, an incorrect identity, and a blocked origin in the learning environment. Confirm that both real-time delivery and reconciliation use the intended protected path.

title: Audit deployment security
text: Audit the access actually exposed by a deployment, then record the changes needed to meet its security requirements.

title: Audit deployment security
heading: Inventory access routes and rules#
text: List client listeners, replication endpoints, node distribution ports, administrative hosts, and load-balancer paths. Compare the configured bindings and network rules with the clients and peers that should reach them.

title: Audit deployment security
heading: Check identities and trust#
text: Inspect users, groups, authentication sources, and grants through the security command reference. Remove unused identities and overbroad permissions. Check certificate names, chains, expiry, private-key permissions, and the clients’ trust stores.

title: Audit deployment security
heading: Exercise the boundaries#
text: From representative client locations, test allowed and rejected connections and operations. Confirm that administrative access is restricted independently of application bucket permissions. Verify that log collection and backups do not expose credentials or private keys.

title: Audit deployment security
heading: Close and verify findings#
text: Apply one controlled change at a time, retain administrative recovery access, and repeat the failed check after remediation. Record the endpoint, identity, operation, expected result, observed result, and date so the next audit can compare the same boundaries.

title: Authenticate an application client
text: Connect an application using the authentication method and trust policy configured for its identity. Keep credentials out of source code and command histories used for production operations.

title: Authenticate an application client
heading: Match the interface#
text: For HTTP, use HTTPS with a trusted CA and hostname verification. For PB, use a client that supports Riak’s security handshake, credentials or client certificate, and CA verification. Do not send plain PB frames to a listener that expects the security handshake.

title: Authenticate an application client
heading: Supply credentials securely#
text: Load passwords and private-key paths through the application’s secret mechanism. For certificate authentication, verify that the certificate identity matches the configured Riak user and source rule. Configure the narrowest grants needed by the application.

title: Authenticate an application client
heading: Test the complete policy#
text: Make a permitted operation against a known key, a forbidden operation, a request with invalid credentials, and a connection with an untrusted server certificate. Verify the application reports each failure correctly and does not retry authentication failures indefinitely. Reopen long-lived connections when testing source or grant changes.

title: Authenticate an application client
heading: Test the complete policy#
text: Verify the application reports each failure correctly and does not retry authentication failures indefinitely. Reopen long-lived connections when testing source or grant changes. Rehearse credential and certificate rotation before expiry; Make an authenticated TLS client connection gives a disposable HTTPS exercise, while Authentication messages specifies the PB authentication exchange.

text: For HTTPS, configure a named HTTPS listener and the certificate paths. For PB, configure those paths and enable security using Enable authentication and authorization; PB does not use a separate HTTPS listener.

title: Configure and rotate TLS certificates
heading: Rotate without losing trust#
text: Distribute any new trust anchor to clients before switching the server certificate. Retain the old trust chain for the required overlap period. Replace the files and restart nodes in a controlled sequence so active listeners load the intended material.

title: Configure and rotate TLS certificates
heading: Verify the served certificate#
