title: Migrate to another storage backend
text: Move data to a different backend by preparing storage that uses the destination backend and copying data through a supported recovery or replication path. A backend setting does not convert existing files.

title: Migrate to another storage backend
heading: Choose and rehearse the migration#
text: Check Backend capability matrix for destination capabilities. For a cluster-wide change, create a separate cluster with the intended backend and use Migrate to another cluster using replication. This preserves the original data while the destination is seeded and reconciled.

title: Migrate to another storage backend
heading: Prepare the destination#
text: Configure the backend before loading objects. Create matching bucket types and properties, provision security separately, and check available disk and memory capacity. Establish real-time replication before seeding so writes during the copy are captured.

title: Migrate to another storage backend
heading: Copy and verify#
text: Seed each required bucket, observe queue delivery, and run reconciliation. Verify known objects, sibling behaviour, data types, and required indexes through the destination’s application endpoint. A matching object count alone does not prove matching values and causal histories.

title: Migrate to another storage backend
heading: Switch traffic#
text: Quiesce or coordinate writers, complete the final catch-up, and switch the application endpoint. Retain the original cluster until the rollback window ends. If writes have reached the destination, a rollback must reconcile those writes back before returning traffic.

title: Remove obsolete Leveled backup files
text: Remove Leveled files that have been explicitly renamed as obsolete `.bak` files after startup recovery. Do not remove active journal, ledger, manifest, or hot-backup files based only on their age.

title: Remove obsolete Leveled backup files
heading: Identify the exact store#
text: Record the node, partition directory, and current backend. Confirm that startup recovery has completed and the files are inside the intended Leveled store. Retain incident evidence if the node recently crashed.

title: Remove obsolete Leveled backup files
heading: Review candidates#
text: List `.bak` files within that store and compare their modification times with the last successful startup. For a cautious cleanup, select only files older than that startup. Review the explicit list before deletion; do not run a broad filesystem-wide wildcard removal.

title: Remove obsolete Leveled backup files
heading: Remove and verify#
text: Delete only the reviewed obsolete files. Check available space, backend logs, and sample reads afterwards. If space does not return as expected, inspect open file handles and retained hot-backup links instead of deleting additional store files.

title: Repair a Leveled store
text: Rebuild a Leveled ledger from its intact journal when the ledger or its indexes are damaged. This procedure does not recover a missing or corrupt journal.

title: Repair a Leveled store
heading: Confirm the recovery source#
text: Identify the affected node and partition from logs. Preserve a backup or snapshot for investigation and confirm surviving replicas can serve the workload while the node is unavailable. Use Repair a vnode or node from surviving replicas if the journal itself is lost or unreliable.

title: Repair a Leveled store
heading: Stop and isolate the ledger#
text: Drain client traffic and stop the node using Start, stop, or restart a node. Under the affected partition’s Leveled store, move the `ledger` directory to a separate recovery location outside the active store. Keep the journal and its manifest intact.

title: Repair a Leveled store
heading: Stop and isolate the ledger#
text: Under the affected partition’s Leveled store, move the `ledger` directory to a separate recovery location outside the active store. Keep the journal and its manifest intact. Do not remove the whole partition directory.

title: Repair a Leveled store
heading: Restart and wait#
text: Start the node. Leveled rebuilds a missing ledger from the journal before the KV application becomes available. Follow `b0006` progress messages and allow time proportional to the stored data.

title: Repair a Leveled store
heading: Restart and wait#
text: Leveled rebuilds a missing ledger from the journal before the KV application becomes available. Follow `b0006` progress messages and allow time proportional to the stored data. Avoid repeatedly restarting a rebuild that is still making progress.

title: Repair a Leveled store
heading: Verify#
text: Check node health, known object reads, and secondary-index queries, then monitor anti-entropy and return the node to client traffic. Retain the old ledger until the recovered state is verified. If rebuilding fails, preserve the logs and use replica-based repair rather than repeatedly modifying the source journal.

title: Schedule Bitcask merges
heading: Configure the window#
text: Check the node’s timezone when defining hour-based windows. Give the window enough time and disk headroom to clear accumulated work. Validate and deploy the configuration through a rolling change.

title: Schedule Bitcask merges
heading: Verify over a full cycle#
text: Observe merge start and completion logs, free disk space, device latency, and request percentiles. If obsolete data continues accumulating, enlarge the maintenance capacity or reduce the workload; repeatedly delaying merges can exhaust disk space.

title: Schedule Leveled compaction
text: Adjust Leveled journal compaction only after measuring its effect on disk use and application latency. Ledger maintenance continues independently and can throttle writes when it falls behind.

title: Schedule Leveled compaction
heading: Establish a baseline#
text: Observe journal compaction scores, reclaimed space, device latency, and request percentiles. In the Leveled logs, `ic003` reports candidate compaction scores and `p0024` helps identify ledger backlog. See How Leveled stores data for the journal/ledger distinction.

title: Schedule Leveled compaction
heading: Adjust scheduling#
text: Choose enough runs to keep disk growth bounded. If a window is required, check the node timezone and stagger it across failure domains. Do not use a journal window as a remedy for an already saturated ledger.

title: Schedule Leveled compaction
heading: Verify the change#
text: Validate configuration, apply the change to a pilot node, and monitor a complete workload cycle. Persistently increasing positive compaction scores indicate work is accumulating; consistently negative scores may indicate that many checks find no worthwhile work. Compare disk and request behaviour before extending the change to other nodes.

title: Diagnose a slow or overloaded cluster
text: Find the constrained part of a slow cluster before changing timeouts or concurrency.

title: Diagnose a slow or overloaded cluster
heading: Bound the symptom#
text: Identify affected operations, nodes, buckets, and latency percentiles. Compare with a healthy interval and recent changes.

title: Diagnose a slow or overloaded cluster
heading: Follow resource pressure#
text: Correlate CPU, memory, storage latency, network use, worker queues, and backend status. Include handoff, compaction, repair, and replication work.

title: Diagnose a slow or overloaded cluster
heading: Test one remedy#
text: Reduce offered load or adjust the identified resource constraint. Keep a comparable workload and record the previous configuration.

title: Diagnose a slow or overloaded cluster
heading: Verify recovery#
text: Check tail latency, errors, backlog, and background completion. A lower request rate without a draining queue does not establish recovery.

title: Diagnose client connection and request failures
text: Separate a client connectivity problem from an authentication, protocol, or application-request failure.

title: Diagnose client connection and request failures
heading: Reproduce at the endpoint#
text: Record the exact host, port, protocol, TLS settings, namespace, method, and response. Compare a direct request with the load-balanced path where allowed.

title: Diagnose client connection and request failures
heading: Check connection stages#
text: Verify name resolution, routing, listener binding, and firewall access. For TLS, check the peer name and certificate chain before checking application credentials.

title: Diagnose client connection and request failures
heading: Check the request#
text: Confirm the bucket type and content encoding, client timeout, and supported operation. Compare the request with the HTTP or Protocol Buffers reference.

title: Diagnose client connection and request failures
heading: Verify both outcomes#
text: Repeat the intended successful operation and a deliberately invalid or denied request. Ensure client retries distinguish uncertain writes from operations that never reached the server.

title: Diagnose missing, stale, or conflicting data
text: Investigate an object that appears missing, stale, or conflicted without overwriting the evidence.

title: Diagnose missing, stale, or conflicting data
heading: Confirm identity#
text: Check the exact type, bucket, key bytes, endpoint, and cluster. A typed and untyped request can address different namespaces.

title: Diagnose missing, stale, or conflicting data
heading: Preserve versions#
text: Fetch the object with its context and siblings. Record deletions, expiry policy, recent restores, and the application’s last successful write.

title: Diagnose missing, stale, or conflicting data
heading: Compare replica and replication state#
text: Check reachable primaries, recent membership changes, repair progress, source queues, and destination lag. Do not assume an empty queue proves dataset equality.

title: Diagnose missing, stale, or conflicting data
heading: Resolve the identified cause#
text: Correct a namespace or client-context error first. Use a bounded repair or an application merge only after determining whether the difference is stale replication or genuine concurrency. Re-read and verify after the change.

title: Diagnose node crashes
text: Investigate an unexpected process exit using the evidence from the failure interval.

title: Diagnose node crashes
heading: Preserve evidence#
text: Save the service exit status, crash dump if produced, system logs, and OpenRiak logs before rotation overwrites them.

title: Diagnose node crashes
heading: Separate causes#
text: Check for operating-system OOM termination, an external stop, resource exhaustion, storage faults, and an Erlang exception. Correlate host timestamps with application errors.

title: Diagnose node crashes
heading: Control recovery#
text: Restore capacity or correct the identified fault before returning the node. Avoid a restart loop that continually interrupts repair or overwrites evidence.

title: Diagnose node crashes
heading: Verify stability#
text: Observe the node under representative traffic and check transfers and repair. If it exits again, compare the first failure signatures rather than treating every restart as a new unexplained event.

title: Diagnose stalled or incomplete replication
text: Locate the stalled stage of a replication path and verify convergence after restoring it.

title: Diagnose stalled or incomplete replication
heading: Identify the generation#
text: Confirm whether the path is next-generation replication or legacy v2/v3, its direction, queue or site, and dataset scope.

title: Diagnose stalled or incomplete replication
heading: Check connectivity and authentication#
text: Test the configured source endpoint from the sink environment. Inspect certificate, credential, and connection failures.

title: Diagnose stalled or incomplete replication
heading: Check delivery#
text: Compare source queue growth, sink worker activity, failures, and source/sink storage pressure. Verify that queue names and filters match.

title: Diagnose stalled or incomplete replication
heading: Recover and compare#
text: Restore the failed stage, observe backlog draining, and perform a reconciliation check for work lost outside the current queue. Verify a known write and deletion at the destination.

title: Diagnose unexpected API responses
text: Interpret the response before retrying or changing data. An unexpected status can be correct for the request that was sent.

title: Diagnose unexpected API responses
heading: Save the exchange#
text: Capture the method, URL, headers, request body, status, response headers, and response body. Remove secrets from shared copies.

title: Diagnose unexpected API responses
heading: Check the contract#
text: Compare with the operation reference. HTTP 204 means successful completion without a response body; an object PUT need not return the stored value unless the supported return-body option requests it.

title: Diagnose unexpected API responses
heading: Check namespace and conditions#
text: Verify bucket type, key encoding, causal context, and conditional headers. A precondition failure, a missing object, and a timeout require different application handling.

title: Diagnose unexpected API responses
heading: Verify the object independently#
text: Fetch the intended object after a successful write and compare its content and metadata. Do not convert every empty body into an application failure or blindly repeat a write.

title: Investigate a running node with Erlang diagnostics
text: Inspect a running Erlang node when ordinary metrics and logs cannot explain a problem. Keep diagnostic scope and duration bounded so investigation does not worsen the incident.

title: Investigate a running node with Erlang diagnostics
heading: Start with inexpensive observations#
text: Record the node, OTP version, workload interval, and symptom. Use Inspect a node through the remote console to open a console, then inspect the relevant process or subsystem through Remote-console interfaces. Avoid dumping all process state or large object values by default.

title: Investigate a running node with Erlang diagnostics
heading: Choose a focused diagnostic#
text: Use process mailbox and memory observations for queue growth, scheduler/runtime statistics for CPU questions, and a narrowly scoped trace only when you know the module or process of interest. Profiling and broad tracing can add substantial load; rehearse them outside production and define how to stop them before starting.

title: Investigate a running node with Erlang diagnostics
heading: Collect and stop#
text: Capture only the interval needed to correlate the behaviour with the failing request. Stop traces and profilers explicitly, detach the console cleanly, and confirm no diagnostic process continues consuming resources. Protect object contents and credentials in captured output.

title: Investigate a running node with Erlang diagnostics
heading: Collect and stop#
text: Stop traces and profilers explicitly, detach the console cleanly, and confirm no diagnostic process continues consuming resources. Protect object contents and credentials in captured output. Compare the result with client and host observations before changing configuration.

title: Investigate a running node with Erlang diagnostics
heading: Collect and stop#
text: Protect object contents and credentials in captured output. Compare the result with client and host observations before changing configuration. Repeat the original symptom check after the fix.

title: Recover a failed node or choose replacement
text: Choose between restarting an intact member, repairing lost storage, and replacing failed hardware. Preserve evidence before clearing data or changing membership.

title: Recover a failed node or choose replacement
heading: Determine what survived#
text: Check storage integrity, node identity, ring metadata, and whether the original process can still run. If data and identity are intact, fix the underlying failure and return the same node without staging a leave or replacement. Wait for hinted handoff and AAE recovery.

title: Recover a failed node or choose replacement
heading: Recover an empty member#
text: If local data is lost but other replicas remain, rebuild the host with the intended identity and compatible configuration. Ensure the old process cannot return. For a new identity use Replace a failed node; for the same identity, stage a rejoin and review the plan before committing.

title: Recover a failed node or choose replacement
heading: Recover an empty member#
text: Ensure the old process cannot return. For a new identity use Replace a failed node; for the same identity, stage a rejoin and review the plan before committing. The plan should not unexpectedly redistribute unrelated ownership.

title: Recover a failed node or choose replacement
heading: Recover an empty member#
text: For a new identity use Replace a failed node; for the same identity, stage a rejoin and review the plan before committing. The plan should not unexpectedly redistribute unrelated ownership. Keep the empty member out of coverage, repair with Repair a vnode or node from surviving replicas, and re-enable protection and routing only after verification.

title: Recover a failed node or choose replacement
heading: Recover an empty member#
text: The plan should not unexpectedly redistribute unrelated ownership. Keep the empty member out of coverage, repair with Repair a vnode or node from surviving replicas, and re-enable protection and routing only after verification. Restoring a stale single-node backup is usually less direct than repairing from current surviving replicas.

title: Recover a failed node or choose replacement
heading: Escalate the recovery scope#
text: If too many replicas are lost, use Recover a cluster after a widespread failure to evaluate another cluster or backup. Do not repeatedly force membership changes in the hope that missing values will reappear. Record which data sources remain available and which time ranges cannot yet be verified.

title: Fold filters
text: AAE fold filters select object namespaces, key intervals, modification intervals, or tree segments. Each operation accepts only the subset shown in its command contract.

title: Fold filters
heading: Bucket and key scope#
text: An untyped bucket is a binary such as `<<"events">>`. A typed bucket is `{<<"type">>, <<"events">>}`. Key intervals use `{StartKey, EndKey}` with inclusive binary boundaries, or `all` where allowed.

title: Fold filters
heading: Bucket and key scope#
text: A typed bucket is `{<<"type">>, <<"events">>}`. Key intervals use `{StartKey, EndKey}` with inclusive binary boundaries, or `all` where allowed. Keep the type when reporting or reusing a bucket identifier.

title: Fold filters
heading: Modified time#
text: A modified range is `{date, Low, High}` using Unix seconds in the underlying fold contract. The convenience `aae_fold/1` interface also accepts supported calendar datetime forms and translates them. These are server modification times, not arbitrary application timestamps or a request for historical versions.

title: Fold filters
heading: Segments and coverage#
text: A segment filter pairs segment IDs with the tree size under which they were calculated. Do not reuse IDs with a different tree size. `n_val` coverage arguments select a coverage plan; using a value larger than the replica count of some data can omit that data.

title: Fold filters
heading: Change method#
text: Where supported, `count` counts candidates without queuing mutations. `local` submits work to the local maintenance path for each participating vnode. Job forms carry the documented job identifier. Do not substitute these methods across operations that have different tuple shapes.

title: Fold filters
heading: Change method#

title: Fold invocation and result conventions
heading: Results and side effects#
text: Read-only folds return collected data or counts. Repair, replication, erasure, and reaping folds can report queued work before consumers have completed it. A count method is non-mutating only for operations that explicitly support it.

title: Fold invocation and result conventions
heading: Results and side effects#

title: Fold invocation and result conventions
heading: Results and side effects#
text: A count method is non-mutating only for operations that explicitly support it. Large listings can consume significant memory even when results are eventually written to a file. Key ranges, modified-time ranges, segments, and coverage values constrain different aspects of a fold; see Fold filters.

title: Fold invocation and result conventions
heading: Readiness and consistency#
text: Initial or incomplete AAE stores can affect results. Concurrent application changes mean a fold is not an atomic snapshot of the whole cluster. Monitor worker pressure and use the smallest scope that answers the operational question.

title: Client compatibility and capability matrix
text: Client compatibility depends on protocol support, server features, authentication, and the language runtime. A client that can read ordinary objects does not necessarily support data types, current queries, or every security mode.

title: Client compatibility and capability matrix
heading: Protocol capabilities#
text: HTTP clients can use the documented Object, datatype, index, Query, and AAE endpoints when the server and policy permit them. PB clients must implement the corresponding message codes and security handshake. Current Query API expressions use their own HTTP contract rather than the legacy PB index request.

title: Client compatibility and capability matrix
heading: Acceptance checks#
text: For a selected library or runtime, verify causal-context preservation, sibling handling, typed buckets, binary values, streaming/continuations, timeout behaviour, and TLS hostname verification. Record the exact client version and OTP/server combination. Do not infer compatibility from an old library’s language name alone.

title: riak_client:aae_fold
heading: Shared arguments
text: `ModifiedRange` `all`date tuple Modification-time filter: `all`, or `{date, Start, End}` with inclusive lower and upper bounds. Each bound can be Unix seconds, or both can be Erlang calendar datetime tuples. The unambiguous datetime 2026-12-24 23:59:59 UTC is `{{2026,12,24},{23,59,59}}` (Unix seconds `1798156799`). For that UTC day: Erlang {date, {{2026,12,24},{0,0,0}}, {{2026,12,24},{23,59,59}}} Use UTC: calendar tuples carry no timezone, and the conversion does not apply a local timezone offset. The Erlang AAE API does not parse date strings directly. To use an RFC3339 string, convert it first with `calendar:rfc3339_to_system_time("2026-12-24T23:59:59Z")`. The shell `riak

title: riak_client:aae_fold
heading: Shared arguments
text: admin tictacaae fold` command performs that RFC3339 conversion itself. Mixed integer/calendar bounds are not converted as a pair. Start must not be later than End. `ChangeMethod` `count``local``{job, JobId}` `count` reports matching keys without changing data. `local` submits the changes to the node-local workers. `{job, JobId}` uses a dedicated job, where JobId is a positive integer, for example `{job, 42}`. The reported match count is not a completion barrier: poll the resulting data before assuming every change has finished. `NVal` positive integer Replication factor of the tree being queried, for example `3`.

text: Step 1: Prepare the example · node1.test Create objects with a fixed historical modification time. This controlled timestamp fixture needs the Erlang API because HTTP writes replace the modification time. Sh riak eval 'begin {ok, Client}=riak:local_client(), TS=calendar:rfc3339_to_system_time("2026-12-24T23:59:59Z"), [begin O=riak_object:new(<<"cli_dates">>,list_to_binary("key"++integer_to_list(N)),<<"dated value">>), MD=dict:store(<<"X-Riak-Last-Modified">>,{TS div 1000000,TS rem 1000000,0},riak_object:get_metadata(O)),

title: riak_client:delete_vclock
heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `Bucket` Argument binary or pair of binaries — Required Not repeatable Bucket — shared argument on riak_client `Key` Argument binary — Required Not repeatable Key — shared argument on riak_client `VClock` Argument vector clock — Required Not repeatable Vector clock obtained with `riak_object:vclock(Object)`. Supply the clock from the object being deleted.

title: riak_client:delete_vclock
heading: Arguments and options
text: `Options` Argument Erlang option list `[]` Optional Not repeatable Supply a list of quorum and timeout options, for example `[{r, quorum}, {w, quorum}, {dw, quorum}, {timeout, 5000}]`. `{r, Value}` and `{pr, Value}` govern the read phase; `{w, Value}`, `{dw, Value}` and `{pw, Value}` govern writing the tombstone. `{rw, Value}` is the legacy combined read/write requirement when more specific values are omitted. `{timeout, Milliseconds}` bounds the operation; `{recv_timeout, Milliseconds}` bounds the caller’s wait. The explicit Timeout argument is also honored by the longer arity. Quorum values accept an integer or `one`, `quorum`, `all`, or `default`; `default` uses the bucket policy. Values cannot exceed the effective replication factor. Timeout values are milliseconds.

title: riak_client:delete
heading: Arguments and options
text: `Options` Argument Erlang option list `[]` Optional Not repeatable Supply a list of quorum and timeout options, for example `[{r, quorum}, {w, quorum}, {dw, quorum}, {timeout, 5000}]`. `{r, Value}` and `{pr, Value}` govern the read phase; `{w, Value}`, `{dw, Value}` and `{pw, Value}` govern writing the tombstone. `{rw, Value}` is the legacy combined read/write requirement when more specific values are omitted. `{timeout, Milliseconds}` bounds the operation; `{recv_timeout, Milliseconds}` bounds the caller’s wait. The explicit Timeout argument is also honored by the longer arity. Quorum values accept an integer or `one`, `quorum`, `all`, or `default`; `default` uses the bucket policy. Values cannot exceed the effective replication factor. Timeout values are milliseconds.

title: riak_client:delete
heading: Errors
text: ConditionResultWhat to do The operation exceeds its configured timeout. The API can return `{error, timeout}`. A timed-out write or delete may still complete on replicas. Check node availability and load. Read back state before retrying a mutation, and choose an appropriate timeout.

title: riak_client:get_index
heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `Bucket` Argument binary or pair of binaries — Required Not repeatable Bucket — shared argument on riak_client `Query` Argument secondary-index query tuple — Required Not repeatable Secondary-index query, such as `{eq, <<"tag_bin">>, <<"blue">>}` or `{range, <<"age_int">>, 18, 30}`. Use an index supported by the backend.

title: riak_client:get_index
heading: Arguments and options
text: `Opts` Argument option list — Optional Not repeatable Options for the four-argument form: `{timeout, Milliseconds}` limits the request; the default is 60000 milliseconds. `{max_results, Count}` caps the result count; `all` is the default. `{pagination_sort, true | false}` requests sorted pagination behavior. Omit it to leave the decision to the index FSM. For example, `[{timeout, 5000}, {max_results, 100}, {pagination_sort, true}]`. Query bounds, return-term selection and continuation belong to the index query definition, not arbitrary extra options in this list. `Client` Argument riak_client handle — Required Not repeatable Client — shared argument on riak_client

text: `Options` Argument Erlang option list — Optional Not repeatable Supply an Erlang list, for example `[{r, quorum}, {notfound_ok, false}, {timeout, 5000}]`. `{r, Value}` is the required read quorum; `{pr, Value}` is the required number of primary-owner responses. `{basic_quorum, true | false}` allows an early failure once the required quorum cannot be reached. `{notfound_ok, true | false}` controls whether missing-object responses count toward the quorum. `{timeout, Milliseconds}` bounds the request. `{recv_timeout, Milliseconds}` bounds the caller’s wait; otherwise that wait is the request timeout plus 100 milliseconds. `{details, true}`, `details`, or `{details, [timing, vnodes]}` requests diagnostics in the result. Quorum values accept an integer or `one`, `quorum`, `all`, or `default`; `default` uses the bucket policy. Values cannot exceed the effective replication factor. title: riak_client:put
heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `RObj` Argument riak_object record — Required Not repeatable Object constructed with `riak_object:new/3`, or an object returned by a read and updated with riak_object accessors. Preserve its vector clock when updating existing data.

title: riak_client:put
heading: Arguments and options
text: `Options` Argument Erlang option list `[]` Optional Not repeatable Supply an Erlang list, for example `[returnbody, {w, quorum}, {dw, quorum}, {timeout, 5000}]`. `{w, Value}` requires that many write acknowledgments; `{dw, Value}` requires durable acknowledgments; `{pw, Value}` requires primary owners. `returnbody` includes the stored object in the result. Without it, a successful ordinary write returns `ok`. `{timeout, Milliseconds}` bounds the request. `{recv_timeout, Milliseconds}` separately bounds the caller’s wait; if omitted, the caller allows the request timeout plus 100 milliseconds. `{details, true}` or `{details, [timing]}` adds diagnostic details to the result; `false` omits them. `{sloppy_quorum, true | false}` controls fallback replicas. `{n_val, PositiveInteger}` overrides the replication factor for

title: riak_client:put
heading: Arguments and options
text: this request; use it consistently with the bucket’s data placement. `{sync_on_write, backend | one | all}` selects the backend policy, coordinator synchronization, or synchronization on all participating replicas. `disable_hooks` skips commit hooks. `asis` preserves the supplied vector clock; it is for specialized replication/import work, not ordinary client updates. `{retry_put_coordinator_failure, true | false}` controls coordinator retry; disable it for operations that cannot tolerate an automatic retry. `{mbox_check, true | false}` controls the coordinator mailbox check. `{counter_op, Operation}` and `{crdt_op, Operation}` carry internal datatype operations; their values must match the datatype module’s operation format. `{if_none_match, true}` requests creation only for a strongly consistent object. Existing causal context selects the consistent update path. Quorum values accept an integer or `one`, `quorum`, `all`, or `default`; `default` uses the bucket policy. Values cannot exceed

title: riak_client:put
heading: Arguments and options
text: the effective replication factor. Timeout values are milliseconds. `W` Argument quorum — Optional Not repeatable Number of successful write acknowledgments required: a count or `one`, `quorum`, `all`, or `default`. `DW` Argument quorum — Optional Not repeatable Number of durable write acknowledgments required. Use a count or `one`, `quorum`, `all`, or `default`. `Timeout` Argument timeout in milliseconds — Optional Not repeatable Timeout — shared argument on riak_client `Client` Argument riak_client handle — Required Not repeatable Client — shared argument on riak_client

heading: Example 3: Update an existing object and read it back
text: Preserve causal context by updating the object returned by get. The w=all and dw=all options require all replicas to acknowledge the write. The API returns ok; a separate HTTP read must return updated value.

title: riak_client:put
heading: Example 3: Update an existing object and read it back
text: The API returns ok; a separate HTTP read must return updated value. Step 1: Run the command · node1.test Erlang begin {ok,Client}=riak:local_client(), {ok,Old}=riak_client:get(<<"cli_reference">>,<<"present">>,Client), riak_client:put(riak_object:update_value(Old,<<"updated value">>),[{w,all},{dw,all}],Client) end. Standard output: Text ok Exit status: `0`. Step 2: Verify the result · node1.test Read present over HTTP with r=all. Expect the newly stored text, updated value. Sh curl --silent --show-error --fail 'http://localhost:8098/buckets/cli_reference/keys/present?r=all' Standard output: Text updated value Exit status: `0`.

title: riak_client:stream_get_index
heading: Arguments and options
text: `Opts` Argument option list — Optional Not repeatable Options for the four-argument form: `{timeout, Milliseconds}` limits the request; the default is 60000 milliseconds. `{max_results, Count}` caps the result count; `all` is the default. `{pagination_sort, true | false}` requests sorted pagination behavior. Omit it to leave the decision to the index FSM. For example, `[{timeout, 5000}, {max_results, 100}, {pagination_sort, true}]`. Query bounds, return-term selection and continuation belong to the index query definition, not arbitrary extra options in this list. `Client` Argument riak_client handle — Required Not repeatable Client — shared argument on riak_client

heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `QueueName` Argument Erlang atom — Required Not repeatable QueueName — shared argument on riak_kv_replrtq_snk `Peers` Argument list of peer tuples — Required Not repeatable List of `{PeerId, Delay, Address, Port, Protocol}` tuples. Address is a string; Protocol is `http` or `pb`. For example, `[{1, 0, "127.0.0.1", 8098, http}]`. An empty list configures no remote peers. `WorkerCount` Argument positive integer — Required Not repeatable Number of concurrent workers for this queue. For example, `2`. title: Repair and recovery commands
heading: Command entry points#
text: `riak_client:repair_node` reconstructs node data from available replicas. `riak_client:aae_fold — repair_keys_range` selects a bounded repair scope. `riak admin repair-2i` is the legacy secondary-index repair family; check backend applicability. `riak_client:hotbackup` exposes the hot-backup interface for compatible backends. `riak admin restore` has its own backup-format contract and is not a generic command for every backend directory.

title: Repair and recovery commands

text: ConditionResultWhat to do No recognised subcommand was supplied. Usage is printed; legacy groups can also return an error term or a nonzero process status. Select a subcommand from the syntax links and provide its required arguments. A joining node uses a different Erlang distribution cookie from the cluster. The local CLI can reach its own node while the inter-node connection fails. The join reports that the destination is not reachable, and the candidate does not enter the staged membership. Plan cannot include that failed join; commit cannot apply it. This message is also possible for DNS, network or node-availability failures, so it does not identify a cookie mismatch by itself. Check the full node name, DNS resolution, network connectivity and the configured distribution cookies. Correct the candidate’s configuration, retry the join, then review the complete plan before committing. A CLI using the wrong cookie for its own node fails earlier; see the shared administrative errors on the parent page.

title: riak admin cluster commit
heading: Errors
text: The candidate node cannot authenticate to the cluster. See Example 3: A joining node has a different cookie.When a joining node has a different Erlang cookie, its join is rejected. Here node5.test uses `cli-different-cookie`; the other nodes use `cli-five-node-cookie`. Run the following join on node5.test. The CLI authenticates to node5 successfully, but node5 cannot authenticate to node1. The join reports that node1 is not reachable; node5 is not staged. That message alone does not distinguish an incorrect cookie from a network or node-availability problem. See shared cluster connection errors. Check the shared cluster connection guidance on the parent page; correct the candidate configuration before retrying. The failed join added no staged member or reviewed plan. See Example 4: Commit after a rejected join.Node5 failed to join because its cookie differs. Run commit on node1: it cannot commit that failed join, and the existing ring is unchanged. Resolve the joining-node connection failure, retry the join, then review the plan.

heading: Errors
text: Node2 is joining, but its plan has not been reviewed. See Example 5: One staged join, without calling plan.Stage node2, then run commit on node1 without calling plan for the join. Commit refuses to apply an unreviewed change. On node2.test, stage its join to node1: Sh VMARGS_PATH=/var/lib/riak/vm.args /usr/lib/riak/bin/riak admin cluster join openriak-kv@node1.test Run cluster plan on node1, review the staged changes, and commit only if the displayed plan is intended.

title: riak admin cluster commit
heading: Errors
text: The staged membership changed after the last plan. See Example 7: Another node joins after the plan was reviewed.Stage node3 and review its plan, then stage node4 before committing. On node3.test, stage its join to node1: Sh VMARGS_PATH=/var/lib/riak/vm.args /usr/lib/riak/bin/riak admin cluster join openriak-kv@node1.test On node1.test, review the node3 plan: Sh riak admin cluster plan On node4.test, stage its join to node1: Sh VMARGS_PATH=/var/lib/riak/vm.args /usr/lib/riak/bin/riak admin cluster join openriak-kv@node1.test Run commit on node1. It refuses the stale plan; nodes3 and 4 remain staged. Run cluster plan again and review every staged node before retrying commit.

title: riak admin cluster commit
heading: Errors
text: The previously reviewed plan has already been committed. See Example 9: Commit again after convergence.The five-node cluster has converged. Repeating commit does not replay the previous plan; the reviewed change set was consumed by the successful commit. No further commit is needed. For another change, stage it and review a new plan.

heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `new_location` Argument text — Required Not repeatable Location label, for example `tokyo-a`. `--format` Option `csv``human``json` `human` Optional Not repeatable Select the Clique output writer. `human` is readable terminal output; `csv` renders tables only; `json` renders structured status records. The launcher can append an `ok` line, so complete stdout is not necessarily a standalone JSON document. An unknown writer warns and falls back to `human`. `--help` /`-h` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Print usage without executing the command. The short spelling is `-h`. `--node` /`-n` Option Erlang node name `local node` Optional Not repeatable Run the operation on the named node, such as `openriak-kv@node1.test`. Use the full Erlang node name. Omit it to target the local node. Do not combine with `--all` where that flag is available.

title: riak admin cluster plan
heading: Errors
text: ConditionResultWhat to do The candidate node cannot authenticate to the cluster. See Example 2: A joining node has a different cookie.When a joining node has a different Erlang cookie, its join is rejected. Here node5.test uses `cli-different-cookie`; the other nodes use `cli-five-node-cookie`. Run the following join on node5.test. The CLI authenticates to node5 successfully, but node5 cannot authenticate to node1. The join reports that node1 is not reachable; node5 is not staged. That message alone does not distinguish an incorrect cookie from a network or node-availability problem. See shared cluster connection errors. Check the shared cluster connection guidance on the parent page; correct the candidate configuration before retrying.

text: Alternate spellings and aliasesThese spellings are retained for historical reference. Use the canonical syntax above in new commands and scripts. `riak-admin describe`

title: riak admin describe
heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `variable` Argument configuration setting name — Required Repeatable One or more configuration setting names separated by spaces, such as ring_size or storage_backend. Do not supply a value assignment. `--format` Option `csv``human``json` `human` Optional Not repeatable Choose the output representation. `human` prints readable documentation; `json` prints an array of text records. `csv` only renders tables, so it omits this command’s setting descriptions. The launcher appends `ok` after successful output. An unknown format prints a warning and falls back to `human`. `--help` /`-h` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Show usage without requesting a setting description. The short spelling is `-h`.

title: riak admin handoff config
heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `--all` /`-a` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Apply to every node in the cluster. Omit it to use the local node or the node selected by `--node`. Do not combine with `--node`. `--format` Option `csv``human``json` `human` Optional Not repeatable Select the Clique output writer. `human` is readable terminal output; `csv` renders tables only; `json` renders structured status records. The launcher can append an `ok` line, so complete stdout is not necessarily a standalone JSON document. An unknown writer warns and falls back to `human`. `--help` /`-h` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Print usage without executing the command. The short spelling is `-h`.

title: riak admin handoff config
heading: Arguments and options
text: `--node` /`-n` Option Erlang node name `local node` Optional Not repeatable Run the operation on the named node, such as `openriak-kv@node1.test`. Use the full Erlang node name. Omit it to target the local node. Do not combine with `--all` where that flag is available.

heading: Syntax
text: Alternate spellings and aliasesThese spellings are retained for historical reference. Use the canonical syntax above in new commands and scripts. `riak-admin handoff enable both``riak-admin handoff enable inbound``riak-admin handoff enable outbound`

title: riak admin handoff enable
heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `direction` Argument `inbound``outbound``both` — Required Not repeatable Choose transfers arriving at the node, leaving it, or both directions. `--all` /`-a` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Apply to every node in the cluster. Omit it to use the local node or the node selected by `--node`. Do not combine with `--node`. `--format` Option `csv``human``json` `human` Optional Not repeatable Select the Clique output writer. `human` is readable terminal output; `csv` renders tables only; `json` renders structured status records. The launcher can append an `ok` line, so complete stdout is not necessarily a standalone JSON document. An unknown writer warns and falls back to `human`. `--help` /`-h` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Print usage without executing the command. The short spelling is `-h`.

title: riak admin handoff enable
heading: Arguments and options
text: `--node` /`-n` Option Erlang node name `local node` Optional Not repeatable Run the operation on the named node, such as `openriak-kv@node1.test`. Use the full Erlang node name. Omit it to target the local node. Do not combine with `--all` where that flag is available.

title: riak admin set
heading: Syntax
text: riak admin set <variable>=<value> ... [[--node | -n] <node> | --all]

title: riak admin set
heading: Syntax
text: Alternate spellings and aliasesThese spellings are retained for historical reference. Use the canonical syntax above in new commands and scripts. `riak-admin set`

title: riak admin set
heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `variable=value` Argument configuration assignment — Required Repeatable One or more assignments, such as `transfer_limit=2`. Values must satisfy the setting’s schema. `--all` /`-a` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Apply to every node in the cluster. Omit it to use the local node or the node selected by `--node`. Do not combine with `--node`. `--format` Option `csv``human``json` `human` Optional Not repeatable Select the Clique output writer. `human` is readable terminal output; `csv` renders tables only; `json` renders structured status records. The launcher can append an `ok` line, so complete stdout is not necessarily a standalone JSON document. An unknown writer warns and falls back to `human`. `--help` /`-h` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Print usage without executing the command. The short spelling is `-h`.

title: riak admin set
heading: Arguments and options
text: `--node` /`-n` Option Erlang node name `local node` Optional Not repeatable Run the operation on the named node, such as `openriak-kv@node1.test`. Use the full Erlang node name. Omit it to target the local node. Do not combine with `--all` where that flag is available.

title: riak admin tictacaae exchangetick
heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `VALUE` Argument milliseconds from 0 to 3600000000 — Optional Not repeatable New value for AAE exchange tick interval. Omit to read the current setting. `--format` Option `csv``human``json` `human` Optional Not repeatable Select the Clique output writer. `human` is readable terminal output; `csv` renders tables only; `json` renders structured status records. The launcher can append an `ok` line, so complete stdout is not necessarily a standalone JSON document. An unknown writer warns and falls back to `human`. `--help` /`-h` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Print usage without executing the command. The short spelling is `-h`. `--node` /`-n` Option Erlang node name or all `local node` Optional Not repeatable Full Erlang node name, or `all` to select all available nodes. Omit to select the local node.

heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `operation` Argument `list-buckets``find-keys``count-keys``find-tombstones``count-tombstones``reap-tombstones``object-stats``erase-keys``repair-keys` — Required Not repeatable Select the range operation. Use count variants before data-removal operations. `nval` Argument positive integer — Optional Not repeatable Replication factor for list-buckets, supplied as `nval=3`. `bucket` Argument bucket name or type/name — Optional Not repeatable Bucket as `bucket=name` or `bucket=type/name`. Required by bucket-range operations. `key_range` Argument `all`FROM,TO — Optional Not repeatable Use `key_range=all` or comma-separated lower and upper bounds. `modified_range` Argument `all`timestamp bounds — Optional Not repeatable Use `modified_range=all` or comma-separated RFC3339 timestamps.

title: riak admin tictacaae fold
heading: Arguments and options
text: `segments` Argument `all`segment-list;tree-size — Optional Not repeatable Use `segments=all`, or a quoted segment list and tree size such as `segments=0,1;small`. `sibling_count` Argument non-negative integer — Optional Not repeatable Sibling-count threshold for key finding/counting. Supply this or object_size. `object_size` Argument non-negative integer — Optional Not repeatable Object-size threshold in bytes for key finding/counting. Supply this or sibling_count. `change_method` Argument `count``local``jobs:N` — Optional Not repeatable For destructive operations, start with `change_method=count`. The runtime also parses local and jobs:N; check the matching Erlang API before using a job mode.

title: riak admin tictacaae fold
heading: Arguments and options
text: `--format` Option `csv``human``json` `human` Optional Not repeatable Select the Clique output writer. `human` is readable terminal output; `csv` renders tables only; `json` renders structured status records. The launcher can append an `ok` line, so complete stdout is not necessarily a standalone JSON document. An unknown writer warns and falls back to `human`. `--help` /`-h` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Print usage without executing the command. The short spelling is `-h`. `--outfile` /`-o` Option filesystem path — Optional Not repeatable JSON destination path on the node. It must be writable by the Riak service account. The short spelling is `-o`.

heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `VALUE` Argument milliseconds from 0 to 3600000000 — Optional Not repeatable New value for AAE rebuild tick interval. Omit to read the current setting. `--format` Option `csv``human``json` `human` Optional Not repeatable Select the Clique output writer. `human` is readable terminal output; `csv` renders tables only; `json` renders structured status records. The launcher can append an `ok` line, so complete stdout is not necessarily a standalone JSON document. An unknown writer warns and falls back to `human`. `--help` /`-h` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Print usage without executing the command. Omit to select the local node.

heading: Arguments and options
text: NameValid valuesDefaultDescription `FILENAME` Argument file path or - — Optional Not repeatable Output archive path. Use `-` for standard output. Omit to use NODE_NAME-riak-debug.tar.gz or HOSTNAME-riak-debug.tar.gz in the current directory. `--cfgs` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Include files from the configured Riak configuration directory, subject to exclusions. `--extracmds` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Include additional, potentially expensive diagnostic commands. Run this selection on one node at a time. `--help` Option Unadvertised flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Print diagnostic-tool usage. `--logs` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Include Riak logs. `--patches` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Include the patch directory. `--riakcmds` Option flag (no value) — Optional Not repeatable Include Riak administrative command output.

title: riak debug
heading: Arguments and options

title: Configuration files, syntax, and precedence
text: OpenRiak uses `riak.conf` for schema-backed settings and `advanced.config` for Erlang application configuration that needs the advanced form. Paths and supported settings depend on the installed package.

title: Configuration files, syntax, and precedence
heading: riak.conf#
text: Entries use `name = value`. The schema determines the accepted datatype, enum choices, units, and constraints. Names containing a placeholder such as `$name` describe a family of named entries; replace the placeholder with the intended entry name.

title: Configuration files, syntax, and precedence
heading: riak.conf#
text: The schema determines the accepted datatype, enum choices, units, and constraints. Names containing a placeholder such as `$name` describe a family of named entries; replace the placeholder with the intended entry name. Commented examples do not set an effective value.

title: Configuration files, syntax, and precedence
heading: riak.conf#
text: Names containing a placeholder such as `$name` describe a family of named entries; replace the placeholder with the intended entry name. Commented examples do not set an effective value. An explicit value remains an override when a later package changes its default.

title: Configuration files, syntax, and precedence
heading: advanced.config#
text: The advanced file contains an Erlang term listing application configuration. It must be syntactically valid, including the terminating full stop. Values in advanced configuration can override schema-generated application values, so inspect both files when diagnosing an unexpected setting.

title: Configuration files, syntax, and precedence
heading: advanced.config#
text: It must be syntactically valid, including the terminating full stop. Values in advanced configuration can override schema-generated application values, so inspect both files when diagnosing an unexpected setting. Keep a setting in one managed location where possible.

title: Configuration files, syntax, and precedence
heading: advanced.config#
text: Values in advanced configuration can override schema-generated application values, so inspect both files when diagnosing an unexpected setting. Keep a setting in one managed location where possible. The schema’s public name and its internal application key need not be identical; the generated catalogue shows the mapping when available.

title: Configuration files, syntax, and precedence
heading: Validation and activation#
text: Use `riak chkconfig` before starting with changed configuration. A syntax check does not establish that a port is reachable, a certificate is trusted, or an existing backend is compatible with a new selection. Restart and runtime-change requirements depend on the setting and its supported command interface.

title: Runtime environment variables
text: Runtime environment variables are read by the launcher, packaging, or service manager. They are distinct from the schema-backed settings in `riak.conf`.

title: Runtime environment variables
heading: Scope and precedence#
text: A variable exported in an interactive terminal is not automatically present in a service started by systemd, OpenRC, or a container entrypoint. The effective environment is the one passed to the running process by that deployment mechanism. The release’s launcher help is available through `riak help` .

title: Runtime environment variables
heading: Scope and precedence#
text: The effective environment is the one passed to the running process by that deployment mechanism. The release’s launcher help is available through `riak help` . Use its advertised options and the installed service definition when selecting an alternate configuration path or execution mode.

title: Runtime environment variables
heading: Scope and precedence#
text: The release’s launcher help is available through `riak help` . Use its advertised options and the installed service definition when selecting an alternate configuration path or execution mode. Do not assume a variable documented for another package controls this launcher.

title: Runtime environment variables
heading: Configuration values#
text: Use the settings catalogue for supported Erlang VM and application values. Environment substitution, service overrides, and direct VM arguments can bypass parts of that configuration path, so record them alongside the managed configuration.

title: Runtime environment variables
heading: Verification#
text: Inspect the service definition and the effective configuration on the intended host. Verify the node identity, listeners, and directories after startup; a variable being present in a shell is not evidence that OpenRiak used it.

text: A bucket type supplies a named property policy for buckets in its namespace. A bucket supplies the second part of the object address; it is not a separately allocated table that must be created before the first object.

title: Buckets and bucket types
heading: Replication scope#
text: Object replication does not provision the receiving cluster’s bucket types or security policy. Matching definitions must exist separately at each destination. Bucket-level overrides and their reset semantics are specified in Bucket property operations.

title: Causal-context and version-vector representations
text: Causal context identifies the versions a client has observed. Treat it as opaque and return it with an update or deletion based on that observed state.

title: Causal-context and version-vector representations
heading: Object interfaces#
text: HTTP returns encoded context in `X-Riak-Vclock`. Protocol Buffers carries the binary `vclock` field. Preserve the value without decoding, truncating, or substituting a client-generated clock.

title: Causal-context and version-vector representations
heading: Object interfaces#
text: Protocol Buffers carries the binary `vclock` field. Preserve the value without decoding, truncating, or substituting a client-generated clock. When resolving siblings, use the context representing the complete observed sibling set.

title: Causal-context and version-vector representations
heading: Data-type interfaces#
text: Distributed data types return their own opaque `context`. Pass it in the enclosing data-type update for operations that remove observed state. It is not interchangeable with an ordinary object’s vector clock.

title: Causal-context and version-vector representations
heading: Limits#
text: Context describes causality, not a wall-clock timestamp or a cross-object transaction. A write without the previous context can be concurrent with earlier versions. A timeout can leave the result uncertain even when the client retained context correctly.

title: Deletion, tombstone, and expiration states
text: Deletion, tombstone retention, and physical reclamation are different object states. Expiration is backend-specific and must not be assumed to have the same propagation behaviour as an explicit object delete.

title: Deletion, tombstone, and expiration states
heading: States#
text: A live object has content and causal history. A delete can leave a tombstone carrying deletion evidence even when an ordinary GET returns missing. Reaping removes retained tombstone state after the deployment’s recovery and replication requirements permit it.

title: Deletion, tombstone, and expiration states
heading: States#
text: A delete can leave a tombstone carrying deletion evidence even when an ordinary GET returns missing. Reaping removes retained tombstone state after the deployment’s recovery and replication requirements permit it. Backend maintenance later reclaims obsolete storage.

title: Deletion, tombstone, and expiration states
heading: Observable behaviour#
text: A missing-object response does not prove that no tombstone exists. Object counts, tombstone counts, backend bytes, and files can change at different times. Removing deletion evidence before disconnected replicas or destinations catch up can allow old values to reappear.

title: Deletion, tombstone, and expiration states
heading: Observable behaviour#
text: Object counts, tombstone counts, backend bytes, and files can change at different times. Removing deletion evidence before disconnected replicas or destinations catch up can allow old values to reappear. The AAE fold interfaces distinguish counting, erasing live keys, and reaping tombstones; their change method determines whether the request mutates data.

title: Distributed data-type contracts
text: Distributed data types accept operations that the database merges across replicas. Their namespace is selected by an active bucket type whose datatype matches the operation.

title: Distributed data-type contracts
heading: Value families#
text: Counter: a signed accumulated integer, updated by increments. Set: unique binary members with context-dependent removal. Grow-only set: unique binary members with additions only. Map: typed fields containing counters, sets, maps, registers, or flags according to the operation schema. HyperLogLog: an approximate distinct count updated by adding identifiers.

title: Distributed data-type contracts
heading: Context and retries#
text: Fetch context before removing observed set members or map fields. A fresh operation can be applied more than once if blindly retried after an uncertain timeout, especially increments. Client identity is not a general deduplication token for these operations.

title: Distributed data-type contracts
heading: Limits#
text: One rapidly updated datatype key can become a hot key. Large sets and maps can accumulate substantial metadata; keep object growth bounded. The ordinary secondary-index Query API does not query fields inside these datatype values.

title: Distributed data-type contracts
heading: Limits#
text: Large sets and maps can accumulate substantial metadata; keep object growth bounded. The ordinary secondary-index Query API does not query fields inside these datatype values. Datatype context and ordinary object vector clocks use separate contracts.

title: Distributed data-type contracts
heading: Limits#
text: The ordinary secondary-index Query API does not query fields inside these datatype values. Datatype context and ordinary object vector clocks use separate contracts. The HTTP and PB pages below define the operations and wire representations.

title: Keys and object representations
text: An ordinary object is identified by bucket type, bucket, and key. Its value is an opaque byte sequence accompanied by content metadata and causal context.

title: Keys and object representations
heading: HTTP addresses#
text: Typed object: `/types/TYPE/buckets/BUCKET/keys/KEY`. Untyped object: `/buckets/BUCKET/keys/KEY`. Data-type value: `/types/TYPE/buckets/BUCKET/datatypes/KEY`.

title: Keys and object representations
heading: HTTP addresses#
text: Percent-encode each path component separately. The same bucket/key under different types identifies different data. A bucket is a namespace, not a filesystem directory.

title: Keys and object representations
heading: Values and versions#
text: The request body carries the value; content type describes its interpretation to clients. Multiple concurrent versions can appear as siblings. Preserve the returned context when updating or deleting an observed version.

title: Keys and object representations
heading: Values and versions#
text: Multiple concurrent versions can appear as siblings. Preserve the returned context when updating or deleting an observed version. Key generation by the server is available through a POST to the key collection; a client-selected key uses PUT to the full object address.

title: Media types and content encodings
text: Object values are byte sequences. HTTP `Content-Type` describes the representation; `Content-Encoding` describes a transformation applied to those bytes.

title: Media types and content encodings
heading: Media types#
text: Use an explicit media type such as `application/json`, `text/plain`, or `application/octet-stream`. The database does not infer a schema or maintain indexes from a JSON document’s fields merely because the content type is JSON. Clients must agree on serialization and character encoding.

title: Media types and content encodings
heading: Encodings#
text: Only declare a content encoding when the stored body actually uses it. Preserve binary bytes when uploading and downloading files. Application-level compression and backend storage compression are separate; backend compression does not require clients to decompress the value they fetch.

title: Media types and content encodings
heading: Siblings#
text: A multipart sibling response can contain different metadata and media types for each version. Decode each part according to its own headers before applying an application merge rule. The resolved object must carry its intended representation metadata.

title: Object metadata
text: Object metadata accompanies each content value. On updates, the application must preserve or replace the metadata it intends to retain.

title: Object metadata
heading: HTTP fields#
text: `Content-Type` and `Content-Encoding`: representation metadata for the stored bytes. `X-Riak-Meta-NAME`: application user metadata. `X-Riak-Index-NAME`: secondary-index terms associated with the object. `X-Riak-Vclock`: causal context for the object state, returned on reads and supplied on context-preserving writes. `ETag` and `Last-Modified`: representation validators and modification metadata; they are not a replacement for the causal-context contract.

title: Object metadata
heading: HTTP fields#
text: Repeated content entries can carry different metadata when siblings exist. A write that changes a JSON field does not automatically change its index term.

title: Secondary-index terms and projected attributes
text: Secondary-index entries associate terms with an object key. A projected attribute is extracted from an index term during Query API evaluation; it is not automatically read from the stored object body.

title: Secondary-index terms and projected attributes
heading: Index names and terms#
text: Binary index names end in `_bin`; integer index names end in `_int`. HTTP uses `X-Riak-Index-NAME` headers, while PB stores index pairs in object content metadata. An object may have multiple index entries.

title: Secondary-index terms and projected attributes
heading: Index names and terms#
text: HTTP uses `X-Riak-Index-NAME` headers, while PB stores index pairs in object content metadata. An object may have multiple index entries. Supported backends and query features are listed in Backend capability matrix.

title: Secondary-index terms and projected attributes
heading: Ordering and ranges#
text: Binary terms use their stored ordering; integer terms require integer encoding. Range bounds are inclusive. For composite binary terms, delimiter choice and boundary construction affect which terms fall within a range.

title: Secondary-index terms and projected attributes
heading: Ordering and ranges#
text: Range bounds are inclusive. For composite binary terms, delimiter choice and boundary construction affect which terms fall within a range. Do not assume locale-aware text ordering.

title: Secondary-index terms and projected attributes
heading: Projected attributes#
text: The Query API begins evaluation with `$term` and `$key`. Its evaluation pipeline can split, convert, and classify the term into additional attributes, then its filter tests them. Define an unambiguous term encoding and test missing fields, delimiter collisions, and conversion failures.

title: Secondary-index terms and projected attributes
heading: Updates and visibility#
text: Send the intended index metadata with an object update and preserve causal context. Changing a value’s JSON fields alone does not maintain corresponding index entries. Index/query results are not a multi-object transactional snapshot.

title: Backend callback interface
text: A storage backend implements the callback contract used by the KV vnode. Capability declarations determine which optional query, fold, and maintenance paths the vnode may use.

title: Backend callback interface
heading: Core responsibilities#
text: The backend starts and stops partition-local state, reads and writes object representations, deletes keys, folds over keys or objects, reports status and size where supported, and handles backend-specific commands. Return forms and state threading must match the release’s behaviour module.

title: Backend callback interface
heading: Capability contract#
text: Capabilities such as indexes, asynchronous folds, native AAE heads, hot backup, and complex queries must correspond to implemented semantics. Advertising a capability without its required behaviour can cause incorrect query or recovery results. See Backend capability matrix for the built-in backends.

title: Backend callback interface

title: Backend callback interface
heading: Versioned definitions#
text: The definitive callbacks are in the release’s `riak_kv_backend` behaviour and built-in backend modules. Compile and test against the exact pinned release source, including missing keys, concurrent access, fold cancellation, restart recovery, handoff, and corrupted data. An older backend plugin is not automatically compatible with a new callback or object format.

title: Cluster metadata interfaces
text: Cluster metadata stores configuration state shared within a cluster, including definitions required to interpret object data. It is distinct from backend object files and from the ring’s ownership records.

title: Cluster metadata interfaces
heading: Scope#
text: Bucket-type definitions, security state, and other distributed metadata must be included in deployment and recovery planning. Inter-cluster object replication does not automatically clone this state into another cluster.

title: Cluster metadata interfaces
heading: Access contract#
text: Use the supported administrative or API operation for the resource instead of editing metadata files or invoking internal storage functions directly. Internal metadata representations and conflict handling are release-sensitive.

title: Cluster metadata interfaces
heading: Backup and restore#
text: Capture ring and cluster metadata with the node configuration and compatible backend recovery set. Preserve node identity, release, and ownership information. Restoring only object files into an unrelated metadata state can produce an incomplete or incorrectly configured recovery.

title: Custom code and hook interfaces
text: Custom Erlang code must match the release’s OTP, object representations, and callback contracts. Code installation and hook registration are separate from ordinary object writes.

title: Custom code and hook interfaces
heading: Code loading#
text: Compile modules for the target runtime and place them in a configured code path available to every node that can invoke them. Verify the loaded module version and avoid replacing a module while incompatible processes are using its old state. Preserve the artifact and source revision with deployment configuration.

heading: Other extension interfaces#
text: Legacy replication helper callbacks use Replication hook interface. Backend implementations use Backend callback interface. These contracts are separate and must not be inferred from a similarly named command-line function.

title: Redis add-on commands and configuration
text: The Redis add-on is a separate integration with its own command and cache behaviour. It must be matched to an identified add-on build and compatible OpenRiak deployment; a standard OpenRiak package does not by itself establish that the add-on is installed.

title: Redis add-on commands and configuration
heading: Integration contract#
text: Check which Redis commands the add-on implements, how it maps keys and values into backing objects, when changes are written through, and what happens when cached and stored data disagree. Compatibility with a subset of Redis operations is not compatibility with every Redis client workflow.

title: Redis add-on commands and configuration
heading: Operational boundaries#
text: The add-on’s listener, credentials, cache memory, expiry, and persistence behaviour are separate from the backing cluster’s object policy. Restarting or losing a cache process must be evaluated against the intended source of truth. Use the specialist setup and application guides only with their matching component source and version.

title: Redis add-on commands and configuration
heading: Operational boundaries#
text: Restarting or losing a cache process must be evaluated against the intended source of truth. Use the specialist setup and application guides only with their matching component source and version. Do not infer a currently verified package or a complete Redis command catalogue from the historical examples.

title: Replication hook interface
text: Legacy replication hooks filter or supplement objects on a `riak_repl` path. They are registered as replication helpers and are distinct from current-generation queue filters.

title: Replication hook interface
heading: Callback contracts#
text: `send_realtime(Object, RiakClient)` and `send(Object, RiakClient)` return `ok`, `cancel`, or a list of Riak objects. `ok` permits the original object, `cancel` suppresses it, and a list sends those additional objects before the original. The first callback is for real-time delivery and the second for legacy fullsync. `recv(Object)` returns `ok` or `cancel` for the received object.

title: Replication hook interface
heading: Execution constraints#
text: Callbacks run within the replication path and must be bounded. Slow external work can delay delivery, and recursive writes can cause feedback loops. Deploy compatible code on every node that can execute the hook.

title: Replication hook interface
heading: Execution constraints#
text: Slow external work can delay delivery, and recursive writes can cause feedback loops. Deploy compatible code on every node that can execute the hook. Intentionally filtering objects changes the expected convergence scope and must be accounted for in monitoring.

title: Replication hook interface
heading: Execution constraints#

title: Write-once interface
text: The historical write-once path optimizes a restricted immutable-object workflow and is deprecated. It is not equivalent to a conditional ordinary PUT.

title: Write-once interface
heading: Policy#
text: A dedicated bucket-type property selects the write-once behaviour. Clients must use unique immutable keys and understand the interface’s acknowledgement and conflict limitations. Do not change an existing mutable workload to write-once merely to reduce latency.

title: Write-once interface
heading: Feature constraints#
text: The path does not perform ordinary coordinated PUT processing and is incompatible with real-time replication of those writes. Do not assume indexes, hooks, conditional updates, or repair behaviour match the normal object path.

title: Write-once interface
heading: Transition#
text: Use ordinary object storage with an explicit key-uniqueness or conditional-write policy for new applications. A migration must preserve the old data and coordinate writers; changing a property or endpoint alone does not prove the existing dataset was converted.

title: Bucket property operations
text: Bucket-property endpoints inspect, override, and reset the policy for one bucket. They do not create or delete its object contents.

title: Bucket property operations
heading: Endpoints#
text: `GET /types/TYPE/buckets/BUCKET/props` returns a JSON object containing `props`. `PUT /types/TYPE/buckets/BUCKET/props` applies a JSON `props` object with the requested changes. `DELETE /types/TYPE/buckets/BUCKET/props` resets bucket-level overrides where supported.

title: Bucket property operations
heading: Endpoints#
text: `PUT /types/TYPE/buckets/BUCKET/props` applies a JSON `props` object with the requested changes. `DELETE /types/TYPE/buckets/BUCKET/props` resets bucket-level overrides where supported. Omit `/types/TYPE` for the untyped namespace.

title: Bucket property operations
heading: Property contract#
text: Property names, types, and defaults are in Bucket properties and defaults. Type-level and bucket-level constraints still apply; not every property is mutable on every active type. Read the effective properties after a change and handle validation errors explicitly.

title: Bucket-type operations
heading: Creation and activation#
text: Use the `riak admin bucket-type create` and `riak admin bucket-type activate` administrative operations. An application’s normal bucket write does not create and activate a new type.

title: Bucket-type operations
heading: Typed buckets#
text: Object paths under a type include `/types/{type}/buckets/{bucket}/keys/{key}`. An untyped path refers to another namespace; it is not shorthand for an arbitrary active type.

title: Conditional requests and latch objects
text: Conditional PUTs test absence or an observed object version before accepting a change. Their coordination is cluster-local and does not provide a formal cross-object or cross-cluster transaction guarantee.

title: Conditional requests and latch objects
heading: Supported write headers#
text: `If-None-Match` on PUT requests creation only if no object is present. This interface treats a supplied header as the wildcard absence check; use `*` explicitly. `X-Riak-If-Not-Modified` carries the encoded vector clock obtained by a prior read.

title: Conditional requests and latch objects
heading: Supported write headers#
text: This interface treats a supplied header as the wildcard absence check; use `*` explicitly. `X-Riak-If-Not-Modified` carries the encoded vector clock obtained by a prior read. It conditions the PUT on that object state.

title: Conditional requests and latch objects
heading: Supported write headers#
text: `X-Riak-If-Not-Modified` carries the encoded vector clock obtained by a prior read. It conditions the PUT on that object state. This is the Riak-specific version check; standard `If-Match` and `If-Unmodified-Since` do not provide the same token-protected behaviour.

title: Conditional requests and latch objects
heading: Supported write headers#
text: It conditions the PUT on that object state. This is the Riak-specific version check; standard `If-Match` and `If-Unmodified-Since` do not provide the same token-protected behaviour. A rejected condition returns `412 Precondition Failed`.

heading: Supported write headers#

title: Conditional requests and latch objects
heading: Coordination settings#
text: Token modes reduce races, but timeout fallback, failure patterns, and ownership changes can weaken serialization. Unconditional writes do not participate in this protection. Concurrent writes in separate clusters do not coordinate tokens with one another.

title: Conditional requests and latch objects

title: Conditional requests and latch objects
heading: Latch objects#
text: A latch is an application-defined coordination object updated with these conditions. Its owner, expiry, and recovery rules belong to the application. A successful latch update does not atomically lock unrelated objects, and an expired owner can still have work in flight.

title: Conditional requests and latch objects
heading: Latch objects#

title: Delete object
text: Delete an ordinary object identified by type, bucket, and key. The operation can retain a tombstone; it is not a request to immediately erase all physical storage.

title: Delete object
heading: Request#
text: `DELETE /types/TYPE/buckets/BUCKET/keys/KEY` Omit `/types/TYPE` for the untyped namespace. Supply the observed `X-Riak-Vclock` when deleting a known state.

title: Delete object
heading: Request#
text: Omit `/types/TYPE` for the untyped namespace. Supply the observed `X-Riak-Vclock` when deleting a known state. Request acknowledgement options use the object-policy contract in Object request options.

title: Delete object
heading: Response and limits#
text: A successful delete returns an empty acknowledgement. A subsequent read normally reports missing once deletion is visible, but concurrent writes or stale replicas need the usual conflict and repair handling. A timeout is not proof that the deletion did not occur.

title: Delete object
heading: Response and limits#
text: A subsequent read normally reports missing once deletion is visible, but concurrent writes or stale replicas need the usual conflict and repair handling. A timeout is not proof that the deletion did not occur. Reaping deletion evidence is a separate AAE operation with stronger retention preconditions.
